title: Esophageal Cancer Surgery: Procedure and Recovery
seoTitle: Esophageal Cancer Surgery | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Esophagectomy removes part of the food pipe and rebuilds it using the stomach. Learn who needs it, how it is done, what recovery involves and how eating.
imageAlt: Surgeon explaining a digestive tract model to a couple in consultation
quickAnswer: Esophagectomy is considered for esophageal cancers that have not spread to distant organs and when the patient is fit for major surgery. It can be done by open, minimally invasive or hybrid methods. Most patients stay in hospital for about one to two weeks, start with liquids or tube feeding, and gradually return to small, frequent meals.

body.text: Esophageal cancer surgery, called an esophagectomy, removes the cancerous part of the food pipe (esophagus) and nearby lymph nodes. The surgeon then rebuilds the passage, usually by pulling up the stomach and joining it to the remaining esophagus. It is a major operation, often combined with chemotherapy or chemoradiation before surgery, and recovery takes several weeks to months.
Who May Need an Esophagectomy?

items: Early or locally advanced esophageal cancer without distant spread
Some cancers at the junction of the esophagus and stomach
Patients who have completed chemotherapy or chemoradiation and are fit for surgery

body.text: Very early cancers may sometimes be treated with endoscopic removal instead.
How Is the Surgery Done?
Open esophagectomy
Uses incisions in the abdomen, chest and sometimes neck.
Minimally invasive esophagectomy
Uses small keyhole incisions with a camera. It may reduce pain and speed recovery in suitable patients.
Reconstruction
The stomach is shaped into a tube and joined to the remaining esophagus. A feeding tube may be placed into the small bowel to support nutrition early on.
What Happens After Surgery?

items: ICU or high-dependency care for a short period
Breathing exercises and early walking to prevent lung problems
Drains and tubes removed gradually
A swallow test before starting oral fluids
Hospital stay of about one to two weeks

body.text: Possible Risks

items: Leak at the join (anastomotic leak)
Chest infection or pneumonia
Irregular heartbeat
Narrowing at the join, needing dilatation later
Reflux and dumping symptoms

body.text: How Does Eating Change?

items: Eat small meals five to six times a day
Chew well and eat slowly
Sit upright during and after meals
Avoid lying flat soon after eating
Raise the head of the bed to reduce reflux
Work with a dietitian to prevent weight loss

body.text: When to Seek Help
Contact your surgical team for fever, chest pain, breathlessness, difficulty swallowing, vomiting or redness around wounds.
Key Takeaways

items: Esophagectomy removes the cancerous food pipe section.
The stomach is usually used to rebuild the passage.
Chemotherapy or radiation often comes first.
Recovery takes weeks to months.
Small, frequent meals are needed afterward.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Esophageal cancer surgery is demanding, but careful planning and an experienced team make a real difference. Understanding each step helps you prepare. For assessment and surgical planning, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: How long does esophagectomy surgery take?
faqs.a: The operation usually takes several hours, depending on the approach and complexity. Your surgeon will explain the expected duration and plan for the hospital stay.

faqs.q: Can I eat normally after esophageal cancer surgery?
faqs.a: Most people return to eating by mouth, but meals need to be smaller and more frequent. Some foods may cause discomfort at first. A dietitian helps you adjust and maintain weight.

faqs.q: Is minimally invasive esophagectomy better?
faqs.a: It may reduce pain, lung complications and hospital stay in suitable patients. The best approach depends on tumour location, stage and surgeon experience.

faqs.q: Why is chemotherapy given before surgery?
faqs.a: Chemotherapy or chemoradiation before surgery can shrink the tumour, treat hidden spread and improve the chance of complete removal. Your oncology team will decide if it is needed.

faqs.q: What is dumping syndrome?
faqs.a: It is when food moves too quickly into the small bowel, causing cramps, sweating, dizziness or diarrhoea after eating. Smaller meals and less sugar usually help.

faqs.q: How long is recovery after esophagectomy?
faqs.a: Most people need several weeks to a few months to regain strength and adjust to eating. Gradual activity and good nutrition support recovery.

title: Stomach Cancer Surgery: Partial vs Total Gastrectomy
seoTitle: Stomach Cancer Surgery | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Gastrectomy removes part or all of the stomach to treat cancer. Learn how surgeons choose between partial and total gastrectomy, what recovery involves.
imageAlt: Surgical oncologist reviewing a stomach CT scan with a patient
quickAnswer: Partial gastrectomy is often used for tumours in the lower part of the stomach, leaving a stomach pouch for eating. Total gastrectomy is usually needed for tumours in the upper or middle stomach or those that spread widely within it. In total gastrectomy, the esophagus is joined directly to the small intestine. Both need lifelong dietary adjustments.

body.text: Surgery is the main curative treatment for stomach (gastric) cancer that has not spread to distant organs. A partial (subtotal) gastrectomy removes the part of the stomach containing the tumour, while a total gastrectomy removes the entire stomach. Nearby lymph nodes are also removed. The choice depends mainly on where the tumour is located and how far it has spread within the stomach.
How Do Surgeons Decide?

items: Tumour location: lower stomach tumours often allow partial removal
Tumour size and spread: larger or diffuse tumours may need total removal
Safe margins: enough healthy tissue must be removed around the tumour
Patient fitness: overall health and nutrition status

body.text: What Is a D2 Lymphadenectomy?
It is the removal of lymph nodes around the stomach and major blood vessels. It helps with accurate staging and may improve cancer control when done by experienced teams.
Surgical Approaches

items: Open surgery: through an incision in the abdomen
Laparoscopic or robotic surgery: through small cuts, which may mean less pain and faster recovery for suitable patients

body.text: Is Chemotherapy Needed?
Many patients receive chemotherapy before and after surgery, called perioperative chemotherapy. This can shrink the tumour and reduce the risk of recurrence.
Recovery in Hospital

items: Hospital stay is often about a week
Early walking and breathing exercises
Gradual start of fluids, then soft foods
Pain control and wound care

body.text: Eating After Gastrectomy

items: Eat six to eight small meals a day
Chew well and eat slowly
Separate liquids from meals by about 30 minutes
Limit sweets to reduce dumping symptoms
Include protein at every meal
Expect some weight loss at first

body.text: Long-Term Needs

items: Vitamin B12 injections, especially after total gastrectomy
Iron, calcium and vitamin D monitoring
Regular follow-up scans and visits

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Partial or total gastrectomy depends on tumour location.
Lymph nodes are removed for staging and control.
Chemotherapy is often given before and after.
Small, frequent meals are needed afterward.
B12 and nutrient monitoring are lifelong needs.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Living with part or none of your stomach is very possible with good planning and support. Understanding the surgery helps you prepare physically and emotionally. For stomach cancer surgery evaluation, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Can you live without a stomach?
faqs.a: Yes. After total gastrectomy, the esophagus is joined to the small intestine. People adapt by eating small, frequent meals and taking vitamin B12 and other supplements as advised.

faqs.q: How long is recovery after gastrectomy?
faqs.a: Hospital stay is often about a week. Full recovery and adjustment to eating usually take several weeks to a few months.

faqs.q: What is dumping syndrome after gastrectomy?
faqs.a: It happens when food moves too quickly into the intestine, causing cramps, sweating, dizziness or diarrhoea. Small meals, less sugar and separating liquids from meals help.

faqs.q: Will I lose weight after stomach surgery?
faqs.a: Most people lose some weight initially. A dietitian can help you maintain nutrition and regain strength with a suitable eating plan.

faqs.q: Is laparoscopic gastrectomy safe?
faqs.a: In experienced hands, laparoscopic gastrectomy is safe for many patients and may offer faster recovery. Suitability depends on tumour stage and patient factors.

faqs.q: Why do I need B12 injections after gastrectomy?
faqs.a: The stomach helps absorb vitamin B12. Without it, B12 levels fall, which can cause anaemia and nerve problems. Regular injections or supplements prevent this.

title: Whipple Procedure for Pancreatic Cancer: What to Know
seoTitle: Whipple Procedure | Dr Varadharajan V
description: The Whipple procedure removes the head of the pancreas and nearby organs to treat certain cancers. Learn who needs it, how it is done, the risks.
imageAlt: Surgical team preparing for a major pancreatic operation in theatre
quickAnswer: The Whipple procedure is offered when a tumour in the pancreatic head, ampulla, lower bile duct or duodenum has not spread to distant organs and can be safely removed. It is complex surgery, best done in experienced centres. Hospital stay is often one to two weeks, and full recovery can take a few months. Chemotherapy is often given before or after.

body.text: The Whipple procedure, or pancreaticoduodenectomy, is a major operation that removes the head of the pancreas, the first part of the small intestine (duodenum), the gallbladder, part of the bile duct and sometimes part of the stomach. The remaining organs are then reconnected. It is used to treat cancers in the head of the pancreas and nearby areas when the tumour can be removed.
Which Cancers Are Treated?

items: Pancreatic head cancer
Ampullary cancer
Distal bile duct cancer
Duodenal cancer
Some neuroendocrine and cystic pancreatic tumours

body.text: Who Is a Candidate?

items: Tumour has not spread to the liver, lungs or abdominal lining
Major blood vessels are free or only minimally involved
Patient is fit enough for major surgery

body.text: Imaging such as CT or MRI helps decide whether the tumour is resectable.
How Is It Done?
After removing the affected organs, the surgeon creates three connections:

items: Pancreas to the intestine or stomach
Bile duct to the intestine
Stomach or duodenum to the intestine

body.text: It can be done open or, in selected centres, laparoscopically or robotically.
Possible Risks

items: Pancreatic leak from the join
Delayed stomach emptying
Infection or bleeding
Diabetes, if pancreatic function drops
Digestive problems needing enzyme supplements

body.text: Recovery
In hospital

items: Close monitoring after surgery
Gradual return to fluids and food
Early walking
Drains removed as healing progresses

body.text: At home

items: Small, frequent meals
Pancreatic enzyme capsules if advised
Monitoring blood sugar
Gradual return to normal activities over weeks

body.text: Why Experience Matters
High-volume centres and experienced surgeons tend to have lower complication rates for Whipple surgery. It is reasonable to ask about the team's experience.
Key Takeaways

items: Whipple removes the pancreatic head and nearby organs.
It is used for resectable tumours in that region.
Pancreatic leak is a key risk.
Enzyme supplements may be needed afterward.
Experienced centres improve outcomes.

body.text: Final Thoughts

The Whipple procedure offers a chance of cure for selected patients. Careful assessment, planning and recovery support are essential. For pancreatic cancer surgery evaluation, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: How long does a Whipple procedure take?
faqs.a: It often takes several hours because multiple organs are removed and reconnected. Your surgeon will explain the expected duration based on your case.

faqs.q: Can you live a normal life after Whipple surgery?
faqs.a: Many people return to daily activities after recovery. Some need enzyme supplements, diabetes care or dietary changes. Regular follow-up helps manage these.

faqs.q: What is a pancreatic leak?
faqs.a: It is leakage of pancreatic fluid from the join between the pancreas and intestine. It is a known risk and is usually managed with drains, antibiotics and monitoring.

faqs.q: Will I need chemotherapy after a Whipple procedure?
faqs.a: Many patients with pancreatic cancer receive chemotherapy before or after surgery to reduce recurrence risk. The plan depends on final pathology and your health.

faqs.q: Why do some people develop diabetes after Whipple?
faqs.a: Removing part of the pancreas can reduce insulin production. Some patients develop diabetes or find existing diabetes harder to control. Blood sugar is monitored after surgery.

faqs.q: Is the Whipple procedure always possible?
faqs.a: No. If the tumour has spread or involves major blood vessels extensively, surgery may not be possible upfront. Chemotherapy may be used first in some cases.

title: Liver Resection for Cancer: Who Is a Candidate?
seoTitle: Liver Resection for Cancer | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Liver resection removes part of the liver to treat primary liver cancer or cancer that has spread there. Learn who qualifies, how the liver regrows.
imageAlt: Doctor pointing to a liver model while explaining resection to a patient
quickAnswer: You may be a candidate for liver resection if the tumours can be completely removed, enough healthy liver will remain to function well, your liver is not severely damaged by cirrhosis, and the cancer is not widely spread elsewhere. Imaging, blood tests and liver function assessment help decide suitability.

body.text: Liver resection, or hepatectomy, is surgery to remove the part of the liver that contains a tumour. It can treat primary liver cancer, such as hepatocellular carcinoma, and cancers that have spread to the liver, most commonly from the colon or rectum. Because the healthy liver can regrow, a significant portion can be removed safely in suitable patients.
Which Cancers Can Be Treated?

items: Hepatocellular carcinoma (primary liver cancer)
Colorectal liver metastases
Some neuroendocrine tumour metastases
Bile duct cancers involving the liver
Selected other secondary liver cancers

body.text: Key Factors in Deciding
Tumour location and number
Tumours must be removable with clear margins.
Future liver remnant
Enough healthy liver must remain after surgery. Surgeons calculate this with scans.
Liver health
People with advanced cirrhosis may not tolerate resection. Other treatments or transplant may be considered.
Spread outside the liver
Limited spread may still allow surgery in some cases, especially colorectal cancer.
General fitness
Heart, lung and kidney health matter for major surgery.
Can the Liver Regrow?
Yes. A healthy liver can regenerate to near its original size within weeks to months after resection. This is why large portions can sometimes be removed.
Techniques to Increase Suitability

items: Portal vein embolisation: blocks blood flow to the part being removed so the remaining liver grows first
Two-stage surgery: removes tumours in two operations
Chemotherapy first: shrinks tumours to allow removal

body.text: Surgical Approaches

items: Open surgery
Laparoscopic or robotic surgery for selected tumours

body.text: Recovery

items: Hospital stay of about five to ten days
Monitoring liver function and blood tests
Gradual return to normal activity over several weeks
Regular follow-up scans

body.text: Possible Risks

items: Bleeding
Bile leak
Infection
Temporary liver dysfunction

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Liver resection treats primary and secondary liver cancers.
Enough healthy liver must remain.
The liver can regrow after surgery.
Chemotherapy or embolisation can expand options.
Liver health strongly affects suitability.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Liver resection can offer long-term control and even cure for selected patients. A detailed assessment shows whether it is right for you. For liver cancer surgery evaluation, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: How much of the liver can be removed?
faqs.a: In a healthy liver, a large portion can be removed if enough remains to function. Surgeons measure the future liver remnant with scans before deciding.

faqs.q: Does the liver grow back after surgery?
faqs.a: Yes. A healthy liver regenerates over weeks to months. It regains function and volume, though its shape may differ.

faqs.q: Can liver metastases from colon cancer be removed?
faqs.a: Yes, in many patients. Liver resection for colorectal metastases can offer long-term survival when all tumours can be removed safely.

faqs.q: Is liver surgery possible with cirrhosis?
faqs.a: It depends on how severe the cirrhosis is. Mild cirrhosis may allow limited resection. Advanced cirrhosis may need other treatments such as ablation or transplant.

faqs.q: What is portal vein embolisation?
faqs.a: It is a procedure that blocks blood flow to the part of the liver to be removed, encouraging the remaining part to grow before surgery.

faqs.q: How long is recovery after liver resection?
faqs.a: Hospital stay is often about a week, and full recovery takes several weeks. Energy levels improve gradually as the liver regenerates.

title: Eating After GI Cancer Surgery: A Practical Guide
seoTitle: Diet After GI Cancer Surgery | Dr Varadharajan V
description: After GI cancer surgery, eating habits often need to change. Learn how to restart food safely, manage common problems like bloating or dumping.
imageAlt: Small South Indian meal of idli, dal and curd on a table
quickAnswer: Start with sips of fluid, then liquids, soft foods and finally regular foods as advised by your surgical team. Eat five to six small meals a day, chew slowly, include protein at every meal and limit sugary or greasy foods. Report vomiting, inability to eat, severe diarrhoea or rapid weight loss to your doctor.

body.text: After surgery on the esophagus, stomach, pancreas, liver or bowel, your digestive system needs time to heal and adjust. Most people start with fluids, move to soft foods and then return to a normal but modified diet over weeks. Small, frequent, protein-rich meals help recovery, prevent weight loss and reduce discomfort.
Stages of Eating After Surgery
Stage 1: Clear fluids
Water, clear soups, coconut water or tender coconut, as allowed.
Stage 2: Full liquids
Buttermilk, milk-based drinks, thin porridge or kanji, strained soups.
Stage 3: Soft foods
Idli, soft dosa, upma, khichdi, curd rice, mashed vegetables, soft eggs, well-cooked dal.
Stage 4: Regular diet
Gradually reintroduce other foods, one at a time, watching for discomfort.
Your team will guide timing based on the type of surgery.
General Eating Tips

items: Eat small meals every two to three hours
Chew food thoroughly
Sit upright while eating and for 30 minutes after
Drink fluids between meals rather than with them, if advised
Include protein: dal, eggs, paneer, fish, chicken, curd
Limit fried, spicy and very sugary foods early on
Keep a food diary to note what causes discomfort

body.text: Managing Common Problems
Early fullness
Eat smaller portions more often.
Dumping syndrome
Avoid sweets and sugary drinks, eat protein and fibre, separate liquids from meals.
Bloating and gas
Limit fizzy drinks and gas-forming foods for a while.
Diarrhoea
Choose bland foods, stay hydrated and report if it continues. Pancreatic enzymes may help after pancreatic surgery.
Reflux
Avoid large meals, eat early in the evening and raise the head of the bed.
Poor appetite
Choose nutrient-dense foods and consider supplements if advised.
After Specific Surgeries

items: Esophagus or stomach: smaller meals, B12 and iron monitoring
Pancreas: enzyme capsules with meals if prescribed, sugar monitoring
Bowel or stoma: chew well, increase fluids, adjust fibre as advised

body.text: When to Contact Your Doctor

items: Persistent vomiting
Unable to eat or drink
Severe abdominal pain
Rapid or continued weight loss
Signs of dehydration

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Eating progresses from fluids to regular foods.
Small, frequent, protein-rich meals help recovery.
Chew well and eat slowly.
Many digestive problems are manageable.
A dietitian can personalise your plan.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Food is a key part of healing after GI cancer surgery. With patience and guidance, most people find a comfortable new eating routine. For surgical care and recovery support, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: When can I eat normally after GI cancer surgery?
faqs.a: It depends on the operation. Many people move from liquids to soft foods within days and to a modified normal diet over a few weeks. Follow your surgical team's advice.

faqs.q: What foods are best after stomach surgery?
faqs.a: Soft, protein-rich foods like eggs, dal, curd, paneer, khichdi and fish are good choices. Eat small amounts often and avoid very sugary or fried foods early on.

faqs.q: Why do I feel full so quickly after surgery?
faqs.a: Reduced stomach size or slower digestion can cause early fullness. Eating smaller portions more frequently helps you get enough nutrition.

faqs.q: Should I take nutritional supplements?
faqs.a: Some people need protein drinks, vitamins or minerals after surgery. Your doctor or dietitian will recommend them based on your surgery and blood tests.

faqs.q: How can I prevent weight loss after surgery?
faqs.a: Eat regularly, include protein and healthy fats, use nutrient-dense snacks and consider supplements if advised. Track your weight weekly and share it with your team.

faqs.q: Is it normal to have diarrhoea after bowel surgery?
faqs.a: Changes in bowel habits are common early on. Most settle over weeks. Persistent or severe diarrhoea, or signs of dehydration, should be reported to your doctor.

title: How Long Does Recovery Take After Cancer Surgery?
seoTitle: Recovery Time After Cancer Surgery | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Recovery after cancer surgery ranges from days to months depending on the operation. Learn typical timelines, what affects healing and how to support a.
imageAlt: Woman resting calmly on a balcony a few weeks after surgery
quickAnswer: Typical recovery times are about one to two weeks for small or laparoscopic procedures, four to six weeks for moderate surgeries like mastectomy or colectomy, and two to three months or more for major operations like esophagectomy, Whipple or CRS-HIPEC. Fatigue may last longer, especially if chemotherapy or radiation follows.

body.text: Recovery after cancer surgery depends on the type of operation, the approach used, your overall health and whether further treatment follows. Minor procedures may need only a few days, while major abdominal or chest surgeries can take two to three months or longer. Energy often returns slowly, and recovery continues after the wounds have healed.
Typical Timelines
Minor or day-care procedures

items: Biopsies, staging laparoscopy, small excisions
Recovery: a few days to two weeks

body.text: Moderate surgeries

items: Lumpectomy, mastectomy, thyroidectomy, laparoscopic colectomy
Recovery: two to six weeks

body.text: Major surgeries

items: Gastrectomy, esophagectomy, Whipple, liver resection, pelvic exenteration, CRS-HIPEC
Recovery: two to three months or longer

body.text: Factors That Affect Recovery

items: Type and extent of surgery
Open vs laparoscopic or robotic approach
Age and fitness before surgery
Nutrition status
Other conditions such as diabetes or heart disease
Complications after surgery
Further treatment like chemotherapy or radiation
Emotional health and support

body.text: Stages of Recovery
In hospital
Pain control, early walking, gradual eating and wound care.
First few weeks at home
Short walks, rest, light activities, follow-up visits.
Weeks to months
Increasing activity, return to work, adjusting to any long-term changes.
How to Support Recovery

items: Walk daily, increasing gradually
Eat protein-rich, balanced meals
Stay hydrated
Take medicines as prescribed
Rest without staying in bed all day
Do breathing exercises
Avoid smoking and alcohol
Seek emotional support

body.text: Prehabilitation
Preparing before surgery with exercise, nutrition and stopping smoking can speed recovery. Ask your team about a prehabilitation plan if surgery is planned.
When Is Recovery Slower?

items: Complications such as infection or leaks
Poor nutrition
Older age or frailty
Ongoing chemotherapy or radiation

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Recovery ranges from days to months.
Major surgeries may need two to three months.
Fatigue often outlasts wound healing.
Walking and nutrition speed recovery.
Prehabilitation helps before surgery.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Recovery is not a race. Every small step forward counts. Following your team's advice and being patient with yourself helps you return to daily life. For surgical oncology care, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Why do I still feel tired weeks after surgery?
faqs.a: Fatigue is common after major surgery as the body heals and rebuilds strength. It may last longer if you are having chemotherapy or radiation.

faqs.q: Does laparoscopic surgery mean faster recovery?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Smaller incisions often mean less pain and a quicker return to activity, though internal healing still takes time.

faqs.q: When can I return to work after cancer surgery?
faqs.a: It depends on the surgery and your job. Desk work may resume in a few weeks, while physical jobs may need longer. Ask your surgeon.

faqs.q: What is prehabilitation?
faqs.a: It is preparing your body before surgery through exercise, nutrition and lifestyle changes. It can improve recovery and reduce complications.

faqs.q: Can I speed up my recovery?
faqs.a: Walking, good nutrition, following medical advice and avoiding smoking help. Rest is important, but long periods in bed can slow recovery.

faqs.q: When should I worry about slow recovery?
faqs.a: If pain increases, you develop fever, cannot eat or feel worse rather than better, contact your doctor promptly.

title: Warning Signs After Cancer Surgery: When to Call
seoTitle: Warning Signs After Surgery | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Some symptoms after cancer surgery are expected, while others need urgent attention. Learn the warning signs of infection, leaks, clots and bleeding.
imageAlt: Woman calling her doctor from home about post-surgery symptoms
quickAnswer: Call your doctor or seek urgent care for fever above 38 degrees Celsius, increasing pain, redness or discharge from wounds, persistent vomiting, inability to eat or drink, severe abdominal swelling, breathlessness, chest pain, leg swelling or pain, heavy bleeding, confusion or no urine for many hours.

body.text: Mild pain, tiredness and some swelling are normal after cancer surgery. But certain symptoms can signal complications such as infection, bleeding, a leak from a bowel join or a blood clot. Recognising these warning signs early and contacting your surgical team quickly can prevent serious problems.
Signs of Infection

items: Fever or chills
Redness spreading around the wound
Warmth or swelling at the incision
Pus or foul-smelling discharge
Wound opening

body.text: Signs of a Leak or Internal Problem

items: Increasing abdominal pain after initial improvement
Abdominal swelling or tightness
Fever with pain
Fast heart rate
Feeling very unwell

body.text: These are especially important after bowel, stomach, pancreas or esophageal surgery.
Signs of a Blood Clot
Deep vein thrombosis

items: Pain, swelling or redness in one leg

body.text: Pulmonary embolism

items: Sudden breathlessness
Chest pain, especially on breathing
Coughing blood
Fast heartbeat

body.text: Pulmonary embolism is an emergency. Call emergency services immediately.
Signs of Bleeding

items: Blood soaking through dressings
Blood in vomit or stool
Dizziness or fainting
Pale skin and fast heartbeat

body.text: Digestive Warning Signs

items: Persistent vomiting
Inability to keep fluids down
No bowel movement or gas with bloating
Severe diarrhoea with dehydration

body.text: Urinary Warning Signs

items: Burning or pain while passing urine
No urine for many hours
Blood in urine

body.text: Other Warning Signs

items: Confusion or extreme drowsiness
Severe headache
Stoma turning dark or black
Drain output changing colour or increasing suddenly

body.text: What Is Usually Normal?

items: Mild to moderate pain improving over days
Tiredness
Mild swelling or bruising around wounds
Small amounts of clear or pink wound fluid
Temporary changes in bowel habits

body.text: Tips to Prevent Complications

items: Walk regularly
Do breathing exercises
Take prescribed blood thinners if advised
Keep wounds clean
Stay hydrated and eat well
Attend all follow-up visits

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Some discomfort after surgery is normal.
Fever and wound redness may signal infection.
Increasing abdominal pain may suggest a leak.
Leg swelling or breathlessness may mean a clot.
Contact your team promptly when unsure.

body.text: Final Thoughts

You know your body best. If something feels wrong after surgery, trust that instinct and call your team. Early action keeps small problems from becoming big ones. For surgical oncology care and follow-up, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Is fever normal after cancer surgery?
faqs.a: A mild temperature in the first day or two can occur, but fever above 38 degrees Celsius, especially later, should be reported as it may signal infection.

faqs.q: How do I know if my wound is infected?
faqs.a: Look for spreading redness, warmth, swelling, pus or foul smell, and fever. Contact your doctor if you notice these signs.

faqs.q: What does an anastomotic leak feel like?
faqs.a: It may cause increasing abdominal pain, fever, fast heart rate and feeling very unwell, usually within days of surgery. It needs urgent assessment.

faqs.q: Why is leg swelling after surgery a concern?
faqs.a: It can be a sign of deep vein thrombosis, a blood clot in the leg, which can travel to the lungs. Seek medical help promptly.

faqs.q: When should I go to the emergency department?
faqs.a: Go immediately for chest pain, sudden breathlessness, heavy bleeding, fainting, confusion or severe abdominal pain.

faqs.q: Should I call my surgeon or go to any hospital?
faqs.a: For emergencies, go to the nearest hospital. For other concerns, contact your surgical team first, as they know your case best.

title: Cancer Follow-Up Schedule After Surgery
seoTitle: Cancer Follow Up Schedule | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Regular follow-up after cancer surgery helps detect recurrence early and manage long-term effects. Learn typical schedules, which tests are done.
imageAlt: Senior patient shaking hands with his surgeon at a follow-up visit
quickAnswer: A common follow-up pattern is every three to six months for the first two to three years, every six to twelve months until five years, and then yearly. Tests may include physical examination, blood tests, tumour markers, imaging and endoscopy depending on the cancer. Your exact schedule depends on cancer type, stage and treatment.

body.text: Follow-up after cancer surgery involves regular check-ups, tests and scans to monitor recovery, detect any recurrence early and manage long-term side effects. Visits are usually more frequent in the first two to three years, when recurrence risk is highest, and become less frequent over time. Many cancers are followed for at least five years.
Why Is Follow-Up Important?

items: Detect recurrence early
Monitor for new cancers
Manage side effects of treatment
Support nutrition, mobility and emotional health
Update you on new evidence or options

body.text: Typical Follow-Up Schedule
Years 1 to 2
Every three to six months.
Years 3 to 5
Every six months to one year.
After 5 years
Yearly, or as advised.
Schedules vary by cancer and guideline.
What Happens at Follow-Up Visits?

items: Discussion of symptoms and recovery
Physical examination
Review of weight, diet and activity
Blood tests, including tumour markers if relevant
Imaging such as ultrasound, CT, MRI or PET-CT when indicated
Endoscopy or colonoscopy for some cancers

body.text: Examples by Cancer Type

items: Colorectal cancer: CEA tests, CT scans and colonoscopy at set intervals
Breast cancer: clinical exams and yearly mammograms
Thyroid cancer: thyroid function, thyroglobulin and ultrasound
Head and neck cancer: frequent mouth and neck examinations, imaging as needed
Ovarian cancer: clinical exam and CA-125, with imaging when needed

body.text: Symptoms to Report Between Visits

items: New lumps or swelling
Unexplained weight loss
Persistent pain
Bleeding
Persistent cough or breathlessness
Changes in bowel or bladder habits
Ongoing fatigue

body.text: Do not wait for your next appointment if you notice these.
Managing Long-Term Effects
Follow-up also helps with:

items: Nutrition and weight
Lymphedema
Bowel or bladder changes
Fatigue
Emotional health and fear of recurrence
Bone health and hormone changes

body.text: Tips for Follow-Up

items: Keep a folder of all reports and scans
Write down questions before visits
Bring a family member for support
Keep track of medicines and supplements

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Follow-up is most frequent in early years.
Tests depend on the type of cancer.
Early detection of recurrence improves options.
Report new symptoms between visits.
Follow-up supports overall well-being too.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Follow-up is your ongoing partnership with your care team. Staying on schedule gives you the best chance of catching problems early and living well after cancer. For surgical oncology follow-up, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: How long will I need follow-up after cancer surgery?
faqs.a: Many cancers are followed for at least five years, and some longer. Your doctor will explain the schedule for your cancer type.

faqs.q: Why are follow-ups more frequent in the first two years?
faqs.a: The risk of recurrence is often highest in the first two to three years, so more frequent checks help catch any changes early.

faqs.q: Do I need scans at every visit?
faqs.a: Not always. Scans are done at specific intervals or when symptoms suggest a need. Too many scans can add unnecessary radiation and anxiety.

faqs.q: What if I feel well? Do I still need follow-up?
faqs.a: Yes. Some recurrences cause no symptoms early. Regular follow-up helps detect them when treatment options are best.

faqs.q: Can I have follow-up closer to home?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Your surgical team may coordinate with local doctors. Discuss options, but keep major reviews with your specialist team.

faqs.q: How can I cope with anxiety before follow-up visits?
faqs.a: Anxiety before visits is common. Talking to family, counsellors or support groups, and preparing questions, can help.

title: Nutrition During Cancer Recovery: What Helps
seoTitle: Nutrition After Cancer Surgery | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Good nutrition helps the body heal after cancer surgery and treatment. Learn which foods support recovery, how to handle appetite loss and when supplements.
imageAlt: Balanced South Indian recovery meal served on a banana leaf
quickAnswer: Focus on protein at every meal, enough calories to prevent weight loss, plenty of fluids and a variety of vegetables, fruits and whole grains. Eat small meals often if appetite is poor. Supplements may be advised if you cannot eat enough. Avoid unproven "anti-cancer" diets that restrict important nutrients.

body.text: Good nutrition is a key part of recovery after cancer surgery and treatment. The body needs extra protein and energy to heal wounds, rebuild muscle, fight infection and cope with chemotherapy or radiation. Eating well can be hard when appetite is low, so small, frequent, nutrient-dense meals and guidance from a dietitian make a real difference.
Why Nutrition Matters

items: Supports wound healing
Maintains muscle strength
Boosts immunity
Improves tolerance to chemotherapy and radiation
Reduces fatigue
Speeds overall recovery

body.text: Key Nutrients
Protein
Builds and repairs tissue. Sources include dal, eggs, paneer, curd, milk, fish, chicken, soya and legumes.
Energy
Prevents weight loss. Include healthy fats such as nuts, seeds, ghee or oil in moderation, and whole grains.
Vitamins and minerals
Found in colourful vegetables, fruits and whole grains.
Fluids
Water, buttermilk, coconut water, soups and juices help prevent dehydration.
Tips for Poor Appetite

items: Eat five to six small meals a day
Keep easy snacks handy, like nuts, fruit, curd or idli
Add protein to familiar foods, like egg in upma or paneer in parathas
Eat the most when appetite is best, often in the morning
Drink fluids between meals so you do not feel full too quickly

body.text: Managing Common Problems
Nausea
Eat dry, bland foods, avoid strong smells and eat slowly.
Taste changes
Try lemon, herbs or mild spices to improve flavour.
Mouth sores
Choose soft, cool foods and avoid spicy or acidic items.
Diarrhoea
Eat bland foods, stay hydrated and limit high-fibre foods temporarily.
Constipation
Increase fluids, fibre and gentle activity.
Are Supplements Needed?

Oral nutritional supplements may help if you cannot eat enough. Vitamin or mineral supplements are useful when deficiencies are found. Avoid high-dose supplements without medical advice, as some can interfere with treatment.
Food Safety

items: Wash fruits and vegetables well
Avoid undercooked meat, eggs and unpasteurised milk
Eat freshly cooked food, especially when blood counts are low

body.text: Avoid Myths

items: Sugar does not "feed" cancer more than other foods in a way that diet alone can control
Avoid extreme diets, fasting or "alkaline" diets without evidence
Balanced nutrition is better than restrictive plans

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Protein and calories support healing.
Small, frequent meals help poor appetite.
Fluids prevent dehydration.
Supplements may help when eating is difficult.
Avoid unproven restrictive diets.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Every meal is a step toward recovery. With patience and support, eating well becomes easier over time. For surgical oncology care and recovery support, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: What should I eat after cancer surgery?
faqs.a: Focus on soft, protein-rich foods such as dal, eggs, curd, paneer, fish and khichdi, along with vegetables and fruits as tolerated. Follow any specific advice from your surgical team.

faqs.q: How can I gain weight during cancer treatment?
faqs.a: Eat small meals often, add healthy fats and protein to foods and use nutritional supplements if advised. A dietitian can create a personalised plan.

faqs.q: Should I avoid sugar during cancer recovery?
faqs.a: There is no need to cut out all sugar, but limit sweets and focus on balanced meals. Extreme sugar-free diets are not proven to cure cancer.

faqs.q: Are herbal or Ayurvedic supplements safe?
faqs.a: Some may interact with chemotherapy or affect liver function. Always discuss any supplement with your oncologist before taking it.

faqs.q: Can I eat outside food during treatment?
faqs.a: It is safer to eat freshly cooked home food, especially when immunity is low. Avoid raw or undercooked items and street food during treatment.

faqs.q: When should I see a dietitian?
faqs.a: If you are losing weight, have trouble eating or have specific diet needs after surgery, a dietitian can help plan meals and supplements.

title: Returning to Work and Exercise After Cancer Surgery
seoTitle: Return to Work After Cancer Surgery | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Returning to work and exercise after cancer surgery is an important step in recovery. Learn when it is usually safe, how to build up gradually.
primaryKeyword: return to work after cancer surgery

about.n: Return to activity after cancer surgery

imageAlt: Woman walking briskly on Marina Beach during recovery after surgery
quickAnswer: After minor or laparoscopic surgery, many people return to desk work within two to three weeks. After major surgery, it may take six to twelve weeks or longer. Start exercise with short walks and build up slowly. Avoid heavy lifting for at least four to six weeks after abdominal surgery. Discuss timing with your surgeon.

body.text: Returning to work and regular exercise after cancer surgery helps restore routine, confidence and physical strength. The right time depends on the surgery, your job, any ongoing treatment and how you feel. Most people can start gentle walking within days, return to light work within weeks and resume more strenuous activity gradually over a few months.
Benefits of Staying Active

items: Improves energy and reduces fatigue
Builds muscle strength
Reduces risk of blood clots
Supports heart and lung health
Improves mood and sleep
May lower the risk of some cancers returning

body.text: Returning to Work
Factors to consider

items: Type and extent of surgery
Physical demands of your job
Ongoing chemotherapy or radiation
Energy levels
Commute and work hours

body.text: Tips

items: Start with shorter hours or a phased return if possible
Discuss flexible arrangements with your employer
Plan rest breaks during the day
Work from home if possible during recovery
Be honest about limits

body.text: Starting Exercise
Week 1 to 2
Short, gentle walks several times a day.
Weeks 2 to 6
Gradually increase walking time and pace. Gentle stretching and breathing exercises.
After 6 weeks
Light strength training and low-impact activities like cycling, swimming (once wounds heal) or yoga, if your surgeon agrees.
Long-term goal
Many guidelines suggest about 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, plus strength exercises twice a week, as tolerated.
Activities to Avoid Early

items: Heavy lifting
Contact sports
Intense abdominal exercises
Swimming until wounds fully heal

body.text: Managing Fatigue

items: Balance activity with rest
Keep a regular sleep routine
Eat well and stay hydrated
Track energy levels to plan your day
Talk to your doctor if fatigue is severe

body.text: Special Considerations

items: After breast surgery: arm exercises help prevent stiffness and lymphedema
After abdominal surgery: protect against hernia by avoiding heavy lifting early
With a stoma: use a support belt for exercise if advised
During chemotherapy: adjust exercise based on blood counts and energy

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Return to work and exercise gradually.
Walking can start soon after surgery.
Avoid heavy lifting for four to six weeks.
Phased return to work helps many people.
Regular activity improves recovery and well-being.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Getting back to daily life is a sign of healing. Listening to your body and building up step by step helps you return safely and confidently. For surgical oncology care and recovery advice, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: When can I go back to work after cancer surgery?
faqs.a: It depends on the surgery and your job. Desk jobs may resume in two to six weeks, while physical jobs may need longer. Your surgeon will guide you.

faqs.q: Is it safe to exercise after cancer surgery?
faqs.a: Yes, gentle exercise like walking is encouraged soon after surgery. More intense exercise should be added gradually with your doctor's approval.

faqs.q: When can I lift heavy things?
faqs.a: Usually after four to six weeks or more for abdominal surgery. Early heavy lifting can increase the risk of hernia.

faqs.q: Can exercise reduce cancer recurrence?
faqs.a: Regular physical activity is linked with better outcomes in some cancers, such as breast and colon cancer. It also improves overall health.

faqs.q: How do I handle fatigue at work?
faqs.a: Take regular breaks, plan demanding tasks for when you feel best, and discuss flexible hours with your employer.

faqs.q: Can I exercise during chemotherapy?
faqs.a: Often yes, with adjustments. Light to moderate activity can reduce fatigue. Avoid exercise when blood counts are very low or you feel unwell.

title: Lumpectomy vs Mastectomy: How to Decide
seoTitle: Lumpectomy vs Mastectomy | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Lumpectomy saves the breast while mastectomy removes it. Learn how tumour size, genetics, radiation and personal preference shape the choice.
imageAlt: Breast surgeon holding hands with a patient during a consultation
quickAnswer: Lumpectomy plus radiation is often suitable for smaller tumours in a single area when the breast can be kept with good appearance. Mastectomy may be advised for large or multiple tumours, when radiation is not possible, in some inherited gene mutations, or when a woman prefers it. Both can be combined with reconstruction options.

body.text: A lumpectomy, also called breast-conserving surgery, removes the tumour with a margin of healthy tissue while keeping most of the breast. A mastectomy removes the whole breast. For many women with early breast cancer, lumpectomy followed by radiation offers similar long-term survival to mastectomy. The right choice depends on tumour size, location, genetics, breast size and personal preference.
What Is a Lumpectomy?

items: Removes the tumour and a rim of normal tissue
Usually followed by radiation therapy
Keeps the natural breast shape in most cases
May need further surgery if margins are not clear

body.text: What Is a Mastectomy?

items: Removes the entire breast tissue
Radiation may or may not be needed
Options include skin-sparing or nipple-sparing mastectomy
Can be followed by reconstruction immediately or later

body.text: Factors That Guide the Choice
Tumour size compared to breast size
A small tumour in a larger breast is more suited to lumpectomy.
Number and location of tumours
Multiple tumours in different areas often need mastectomy.
Ability to have radiation
Lumpectomy usually needs radiation. Previous chest radiation or pregnancy may affect this.
Genetic risk
Women with BRCA mutations may consider mastectomy, sometimes of both breasts.
Personal preference
Some women prefer to keep their breast; others prefer mastectomy for peace of mind. Both are valid.
Can Chemotherapy Help Preserve the Breast?
In some cases, chemotherapy before surgery can shrink a large tumour enough to allow lumpectomy.
Does Mastectomy Mean Lower Recurrence?
For suitable early cancers, lumpectomy with radiation and mastectomy have similar survival outcomes. Local recurrence rates may vary slightly, but survival is comparable.
Recovery Differences

items: Lumpectomy: shorter recovery, followed by several weeks of radiation
Mastectomy: longer recovery, drains may be needed, possible reconstruction

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Lumpectomy saves the breast; mastectomy removes it.
Survival is similar for many early cancers.
Tumour size, number and genetics matter.
Radiation usually follows lumpectomy.
Personal preference is an important factor.

body.text: Final Thoughts

There is no single right answer for every woman. Understanding your options and discussing them openly helps you make a confident decision. For breast cancer surgery planning, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Is lumpectomy as safe as mastectomy?
faqs.a: For many early breast cancers, lumpectomy followed by radiation provides similar long-term survival to mastectomy. Your surgeon will advise if you are a suitable candidate.

faqs.q: Do I always need radiation after lumpectomy?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes. Radiation reduces the risk of the cancer returning in the breast. Some older women with very low-risk tumours may be able to skip it after discussion.

faqs.q: Can I have breast reconstruction after mastectomy?
faqs.a: Yes. Reconstruction can be done at the same time or later, using implants or your own tissue. Your surgeon will discuss options suited to you.

faqs.q: What does clear margins mean?
faqs.a: It means no cancer cells are seen at the edges of the removed tissue. If margins are not clear, further surgery may be needed.

faqs.q: Should women with BRCA mutations have mastectomy?
faqs.a: Many consider it because of higher risk of new cancers. The decision is personal and should be made with genetic counselling and your surgical team.

faqs.q: Can chemotherapy before surgery help avoid mastectomy?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Chemotherapy can shrink a large tumour, making breast-conserving surgery possible. Your oncology team will assess if this applies to you.

title: What Is Oncoplastic Breast Surgery?
seoTitle: Oncoplastic Breast Surgery | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Oncoplastic surgery combines cancer removal with plastic surgery techniques to preserve breast shape. Learn how it works, who may benefit and what results to.
imageAlt: Confident woman standing by a window after breast surgery recovery
quickAnswer: Oncoplastic surgery reshapes the remaining breast tissue after the tumour is removed, or uses nearby tissue to fill the gap. It may include a breast lift or reduction, and sometimes surgery on the other breast for symmetry. It is suitable for many women having breast-conserving surgery, especially when a standard lumpectomy would leave a dent or uneven shape.

body.text: Oncoplastic breast surgery combines breast cancer removal with plastic surgery techniques in the same operation. The goal is to remove the cancer completely while preserving or restoring a natural breast shape. It allows some women to have breast-conserving surgery even with larger tumours and reduces deformity after lumpectomy.
Why Is It Done?

items: To remove cancer with clear margins
To avoid dents or distortion after lumpectomy
To allow breast conservation for larger tumours
To improve symmetry between both breasts
To support confidence and quality of life

body.text: Types of Oncoplastic Techniques
Volume displacement
Remaining breast tissue is rearranged to fill the space left by the tumour. Often combined with a breast lift or reduction pattern.
Volume replacement
Tissue from nearby areas, such as the side of the chest, is moved to fill the gap.
Symmetry surgery
The other breast may be lifted or reduced to match.
Who May Benefit?

items: Women with medium to large tumours relative to breast size
Tumours in areas where a lumpectomy would distort shape
Women with larger or drooping breasts
Those who want to keep their breast with good appearance

body.text: Who May Not Be Suitable?

items: Very large or multiple tumours needing mastectomy
Women who cannot have radiation
Certain health conditions affecting healing

body.text: Is It Safe From a Cancer Point of View?

Yes. Oncoplastic surgery follows the same cancer principles as standard surgery. It often allows wider margins because the defect is reconstructed. Radiation usually follows, as with standard lumpectomy.
Recovery

items: Hospital stay of one to two days in many cases
Supportive bra for several weeks
Return to light activity within one to two weeks
Radiation usually begins after healing

body.text: Possible Risks

items: Wound healing problems
Changes in nipple sensation
Asymmetry needing further adjustment
Fat necrosis, which feels like a lump but is not cancer

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Oncoplastic surgery combines cancer and plastic techniques.
It helps preserve natural breast shape.
It may allow conservation of larger tumours.
Symmetry surgery on the other breast is possible.
Cancer safety remains the priority.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Oncoplastic surgery reflects a whole-person approach to breast cancer care. It treats the cancer while caring for how you feel about your body afterward. For breast cancer and oncoplastic surgery assessment, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: What is the difference between lumpectomy and oncoplastic surgery?
faqs.a: A standard lumpectomy removes the tumour. Oncoplastic surgery removes the tumour and reshapes the breast in the same operation to preserve a natural appearance.

faqs.q: Will I need radiation after oncoplastic surgery?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Radiation is typically given after breast-conserving surgery, including oncoplastic surgery, to lower recurrence risk.

faqs.q: Can oncoplastic surgery be done on both breasts?
faqs.a: Yes. Sometimes the other breast is reshaped at the same time or later to improve symmetry.

faqs.q: Is oncoplastic surgery more painful?
faqs.a: Recovery may be slightly longer than a simple lumpectomy because more tissue is reshaped. Pain is usually well controlled with medicines.

faqs.q: Does oncoplastic surgery affect cancer outcomes?
faqs.a: It follows standard cancer principles and often allows wide margins. Outcomes are similar to standard breast-conserving surgery when performed appropriately.

faqs.q: Will my breast look natural afterward?
faqs.a: Many women are happy with the appearance after oncoplastic surgery. Some changes in shape or size are expected, and minor adjustments may be done later if needed.

title: Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy in Breast Cancer
seoTitle: Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Sentinel node biopsy checks whether breast cancer has spread to the armpit by removing only the first few nodes. Learn how it works and why it lowers.
imageAlt: Patient speaking with a surgeon beside a hospital bed before biopsy
quickAnswer: SLNB uses a dye, a radioactive tracer or both to identify the sentinel nodes. These are removed and examined. If they show no cancer, further node removal is usually not needed. If cancer is found, the team decides whether more surgery, radiation or other treatment is required. SLNB is standard for most early breast cancers with no obviously enlarged nodes.

body.text: Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) is a procedure to check whether breast cancer has spread to the lymph nodes in the armpit. Instead of removing many nodes, the surgeon finds and removes the first one to three nodes that drain the breast, called sentinel nodes. If these are free of cancer, the rest are usually left alone, which lowers the risk of arm swelling (lymphedema).
Why Are Lymph Nodes Checked?
Lymph nodes are often the first place breast cancer spreads. Knowing whether nodes are involved helps:

items: Stage the cancer accurately
Decide on chemotherapy, radiation or hormone treatment
Plan further surgery if needed

body.text: How Is SLNB Done?

items: A blue dye, a radioactive tracer or both are injected near the tumour or nipple
The tracer travels to the sentinel nodes
During surgery, the surgeon locates the coloured or radioactive nodes
One to three nodes are usually removed through a small cut in the armpit
Nodes are examined by a pathologist

body.text: It is often done at the same time as lumpectomy or mastectomy.
SLNB vs Axillary Lymph Node Dissection

items: SLNB: removes a few nodes, lower risk of lymphedema, quicker recovery
Axillary dissection: removes many nodes, higher risk of arm swelling and stiffness, used when nodes are clearly involved

body.text: Who Is Suitable for SLNB?

items: Early breast cancer
No obviously enlarged or cancerous nodes on exam or imaging
Some patients after chemotherapy, depending on response

body.text: What Are the Risks?

items: Mild pain or numbness in the armpit
Temporary blue discolouration of skin or urine from the dye
Rare allergic reaction to dye
Small risk of lymphedema, much lower than with full dissection
Fluid collection (seroma)

body.text: Recovery

items: Most people return to light activities within days
Gentle arm exercises help prevent stiffness
Watch for swelling, redness or fever

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: SLNB removes only the first few nodes.
It accurately stages most early breast cancers.
It lowers the risk of lymphedema.
Dye or tracer helps find the nodes.
Results guide further treatment.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Sentinel node biopsy is a major advance that spares many women from extensive armpit surgery. Understanding it can ease anxiety before your operation. For breast cancer surgery planning, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: What is a sentinel lymph node?
faqs.a: It is the first lymph node or group of nodes that drains fluid from the breast. If cancer spreads, it is likely to reach these nodes first.

faqs.q: Is sentinel node biopsy painful?
faqs.a: It is done under anaesthesia during breast surgery. Afterwards, mild pain or numbness in the armpit is common and usually improves within weeks.

faqs.q: What happens if the sentinel node has cancer?
faqs.a: Your team will decide whether more nodes need removal, or if radiation and other treatments are enough. Many women with limited node involvement can avoid full dissection.

faqs.q: Why does my urine look blue after surgery?
faqs.a: Blue dye used to find sentinel nodes can pass into the urine and make it blue or green for a day or two. This is harmless.

faqs.q: Does SLNB cause lymphedema?
faqs.a: The risk is much lower than with full axillary dissection, but it is not zero. Arm care and early reporting of swelling help.

faqs.q: Can SLNB be done after chemotherapy?
faqs.a: In some cases, yes. The decision depends on node status before and after chemotherapy. Your surgical team will explain if it applies to you.

title: Breast Lump: When to Worry and Which Tests Help
seoTitle: Breast Lump Causes | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Most breast lumps are not cancer, but every new lump should be checked. Learn the warning signs, common harmless causes and the tests doctors use to find the.
imageAlt: Woman holding a referral slip in a clinic waiting area
quickAnswer: See a doctor promptly for any new breast or armpit lump, especially if it is hard, painless, fixed, growing, or comes with skin dimpling, nipple changes or bloody discharge. Evaluation usually includes a breast exam, ultrasound and/or mammogram, and a core needle biopsy if the imaging is suspicious.

body.text: Finding a breast lump can be frightening, but most breast lumps are not cancer. Common harmless causes include fibroadenomas, cysts and hormonal changes. Still, every new or changing lump should be checked by a doctor, because early breast cancer is very treatable. Doctors usually use a clinical exam, imaging and, if needed, a needle biopsy to find the cause.
Common Non-Cancerous Causes

items: Fibroadenoma: smooth, rubbery, movable lump, common in younger women
Cysts: fluid-filled lumps that may be tender
Fibrocystic changes: lumpy, tender breasts around periods
Infection or abscess: painful, red, warm lump, often during breastfeeding
Fat necrosis: firm lump after injury or surgery

body.text: Warning Signs That Need Prompt Assessment

items: Hard, irregular, painless lump
Lump that is fixed to the skin or chest wall
Lump that is growing
Skin dimpling, puckering or orange-peel texture
Nipple turning inward recently
Bloody nipple discharge
Redness or swelling of the breast without infection
Lump in the armpit

body.text: Tests Used to Evaluate a Lump
Clinical breast examination
A doctor examines both breasts and armpits.
Ultrasound
Often the first test for women under 40. It shows whether a lump is solid or fluid-filled.
Mammogram
Usually used for women over 40, sometimes with ultrasound.
Core needle biopsy
A small tissue sample is taken with a needle under local anaesthesia, often guided by ultrasound. This confirms the diagnosis.
Fine needle aspiration
Used for cysts or some lumps.
MRI
Used in selected cases, such as high-risk women or unclear findings.
What Is the Triple Assessment?
Doctors combine clinical examination, imaging and biopsy to reach a reliable diagnosis. This approach reduces the chance of missing cancer.
What If the Lump Is Cancer?
Your doctor will arrange staging tests and discuss treatment, which may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, hormone or targeted therapy. Early diagnosis gives more treatment options.
Key Takeaways

items: Most breast lumps are not cancer.
Every new lump should still be checked.
Hard, fixed or growing lumps need prompt review.
Ultrasound, mammogram and biopsy confirm the cause.
Early diagnosis improves treatment outcomes.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Checking a lump early is an act of self-care, not fear. Most results bring reassurance, and if cancer is found, early treatment works best. For breast lump assessment, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Are painful breast lumps less likely to be cancer?
faqs.a: Painful lumps are often caused by cysts or hormonal changes, but pain does not rule out cancer. Any new or persistent lump should be checked.

faqs.q: Can young women get breast cancer?
faqs.a: Yes, though it is less common. Breast lumps in young women are often fibroadenomas, but they still need evaluation, especially if they grow or feel hard.

faqs.q: Is a biopsy painful?
faqs.a: A core needle biopsy is done under local anaesthesia. Most women feel pressure rather than pain. Mild bruising or soreness afterwards is common.

faqs.q: Can a biopsy spread cancer?
faqs.a: No. A needle biopsy does not cause cancer to spread. It is a safe and essential step for accurate diagnosis.

faqs.q: What is a fibroadenoma?
faqs.a: It is a common non-cancerous breast lump, usually smooth, firm and movable. Many do not need removal but should be monitored.

faqs.q: Should I wait to see if a lump goes away?
faqs.a: If a lump changes with your cycle, your doctor may re-check after a period. However, a lump that persists or grows should be evaluated promptly.

title: Recovery After Breast Cancer Surgery and Lymphedema
seoTitle: Recovery After Breast Surgery | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Recovery after breast cancer surgery involves wound care, drains, arm exercises and watching for lymphedema. Learn what to expect week by week.
imageAlt: Patient doing shoulder exercises with a physiotherapist after surgery
quickAnswer: After surgery, expect mild pain, tightness and fatigue. Drains, if used, are often removed within one to two weeks. Begin gentle arm exercises as advised to prevent stiffness. Protect the arm on the operated side from injury and infection, and report any swelling, heaviness or redness early, as lymphedema is easier to manage when caught early.

body.text: Most women recover from breast cancer surgery within a few weeks, though full healing can take longer, especially after mastectomy or lymph node removal. Recovery includes wound and drain care, gentle arm exercises to restore movement and steps to lower the risk of lymphedema, which is swelling of the arm caused by changes in lymph drainage.
The First Few Days

items: Pain relief as prescribed
Wearing a supportive, soft bra
Keeping wounds clean and dry
Short walks to prevent clots
Learning to care for drains if present

body.text: Weeks 1 to 2

items: Drains are usually removed
Gentle shoulder and arm exercises begin
Light household activity is often allowed
Avoid lifting heavy objects
First follow-up and discussion of pathology results

body.text: Weeks 3 to 6

items: Arm movement improves with exercise
Return to work for many women, depending on job type
Further treatment, such as radiation or chemotherapy, may start

body.text: What Is Lymphedema?

Lymphedema is swelling of the arm, hand, breast or chest wall caused by a build-up of lymph fluid after lymph nodes are removed or treated with radiation. It can appear months or even years after treatment.
Early signs

items: Heaviness or tightness in the arm
Rings or bangles feeling tight
Swelling in the hand or arm
Reduced flexibility

body.text: How to Lower Lymphedema Risk

items: Do recommended arm exercises
Maintain a healthy weight
Avoid cuts, burns and insect bites on that arm
Use gloves for gardening or cleaning
Moisturise skin to prevent cracks
Treat infections promptly
Increase heavy lifting gradually with guidance

body.text: How Is Lymphedema Managed?

items: Manual lymphatic drainage by a trained therapist
Compression sleeves
Exercise and skin care
Early treatment for infections

body.text: When to Call Your Doctor

items: Redness, warmth or swelling of the wound or arm
Fever
Fluid collecting under the wound (seroma)
Sudden increase in arm swelling

body.text: Emotional Recovery
Changes in body image, fatigue and worry are common. Support groups, counselling and open conversations with loved ones help.
Key Takeaways

items: Most women recover within a few weeks.
Arm exercises prevent stiffness.
Lymphedema can appear months or years later.
Protect the arm from injury and infection.
Report swelling early for best results.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Recovery involves both the body and the mind. With good care and support, most women return to their normal lives with confidence. For surgical follow-up and recovery guidance, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: How long does it take to recover from breast cancer surgery?
faqs.a: Many women recover from lumpectomy in one to two weeks and from mastectomy in three to six weeks. Recovery may take longer if lymph nodes are removed or reconstruction is done.

faqs.q: When are surgical drains removed?
faqs.a: Drains are usually removed when fluid output drops, often within one to two weeks. Your team will give you instructions for drain care at home.

faqs.q: Can I lift my arm after surgery?
faqs.a: Gentle movement is encouraged early, but heavy lifting should be avoided initially. Follow your surgeon's or physiotherapist's exercise plan.

faqs.q: Is lymphedema permanent?
faqs.a: Lymphedema can be long-term, but early treatment helps control swelling and symptoms. Compression, exercise and therapy make a big difference.

faqs.q: Can I have blood tests or BP checks on the operated arm?
faqs.a: Many teams advise using the other arm when possible, especially after axillary dissection. Ask your doctor for personalised advice.

faqs.q: When can I return to exercise?
faqs.a: Light walking can start early. More strenuous exercise is usually resumed gradually over weeks, guided by your doctor. Supervised exercise can lower lymphedema risk.

title: Ovarian Cancer Symptoms Women Often Miss
seoTitle: Ovarian Cancer Symptoms | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Ovarian cancer often causes vague symptoms like bloating and early fullness. Learn the warning signs that persist, who is at higher risk and which tests help.
imageAlt: Woman holding her lower abdomen while sitting on a sofa at home
quickAnswer: See a doctor if you have persistent bloating, a swollen abdomen, pelvic or tummy pain, early fullness or loss of appetite, or needing to urinate more often, especially if you are over 50 or have a family history of ovarian or breast cancer. Tests usually include a pelvic examination, ultrasound and a CA-125 blood test.

body.text: Ovarian cancer is often called a silent disease because early symptoms are vague and easy to mistake for digestive problems. The key warning signs are bloating, pelvic or abdominal pain, feeling full quickly and urinary urgency that are new, persistent and happen most days for more than a few weeks. Recognising this pattern and getting checked early can lead to earlier diagnosis.
Commonly Missed Symptoms

items: Persistent bloating or a feeling of swelling
Increasing waist size or clothes feeling tight
Pain in the lower abdomen or pelvis
Feeling full quickly after small meals
Loss of appetite
Needing to urinate urgently or frequently
Change in bowel habits
Tiredness without clear reason
Back pain
Unexplained weight loss or gain

body.text: Why Are They Missed?

These symptoms are common with gas, acidity, irritable bowel or urinary infections. Many women self-treat or delay seeing a doctor. The difference is persistence: ovarian cancer symptoms are usually new, frequent and continue for weeks.
Who Is at Higher Risk?

items: Women over 50 or after menopause
Family history of ovarian, breast or colon cancer
BRCA1, BRCA2 or Lynch syndrome gene changes
Endometriosis
Never having been pregnant
Obesity

body.text: How Is It Evaluated?

items: Pelvic examination
Transvaginal ultrasound: checks the ovaries for masses or cysts
CA-125 blood test: may be raised in ovarian cancer, but also in other conditions
CT or MRI: to assess spread if a suspicious mass is found
Surgery or biopsy: confirms the diagnosis

body.text: Is There a Screening Test?

There is currently no reliable screening test for ovarian cancer in women at average risk. Women with high genetic risk may need specialised monitoring or preventive surgery discussed with a specialist.
How Is Ovarian Cancer Treated?

Treatment usually involves surgery to remove the tumour and as much cancer as possible, along with chemotherapy. In some advanced cases, chemotherapy is given first. Selected cases with peritoneal spread may be considered for cytoreductive surgery.
Key Takeaways

items: Early ovarian cancer symptoms are vague.
Persistence over weeks is the key clue.
Bloating, pain and early fullness are common signs.
Family history and BRCA genes raise risk.
Ultrasound and CA-125 help evaluation.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Listening to persistent changes in your body can make a real difference. If symptoms do not settle, ask for a proper evaluation. For gynecological oncology assessment, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: What is the first sign of ovarian cancer?
faqs.a: Persistent bloating or abdominal swelling is often one of the earliest signs. Pelvic pain, early fullness and urinary urgency are also common. Symptoms that last weeks should be checked.

faqs.q: Can a normal CA-125 rule out ovarian cancer?
faqs.a: No. CA-125 can be normal in some early ovarian cancers and raised in non-cancerous conditions. It is used together with ultrasound and clinical findings.

faqs.q: Is there a screening test for ovarian cancer?
faqs.a: There is no proven screening test for women at average risk. Women with high genetic risk should discuss monitoring and preventive options with a specialist.

faqs.q: Can young women get ovarian cancer?
faqs.a: Yes, though it is more common after 50. Some ovarian tumours, such as germ cell tumours, occur in younger women. Persistent symptoms at any age should be evaluated.

faqs.q: Do ovarian cysts mean cancer?
faqs.a: Most ovarian cysts are harmless, especially in younger women. Ultrasound features help doctors decide whether a cyst needs monitoring, further tests or removal.

faqs.q: Is ovarian cancer hereditary?
faqs.a: Some cases are linked to inherited gene changes such as BRCA1, BRCA2 or Lynch syndrome. Women with a strong family history may benefit from genetic counselling.

title: Cervical Cancer Stages and Treatment Options
seoTitle: Cervical Cancer Stages | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Cervical cancer treatment depends on stage, from minor surgery for early disease to chemoradiation for advanced cancer. Learn the stages, options.
imageAlt: Gynecologic oncologist explaining cervical cancer stages on a scan
quickAnswer: Stage 1 cancers are usually treated with surgery such as cone biopsy, simple or radical hysterectomy. Stage 2 and 3 cancers are often treated with chemoradiation, which combines radiation and chemotherapy. Stage 4 cancers, which have spread to nearby organs or distant sites, are treated with chemotherapy, radiation and newer therapies to control disease and symptoms.

body.text: Cervical cancer starts in the cervix, the lower part of the uterus, and is mostly caused by long-term infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV). Treatment depends on the stage. Early-stage cancer is often treated with surgery, while more advanced stages are usually treated with combined chemotherapy and radiation. When found early, cervical cancer is highly treatable.
Common Symptoms

items: Bleeding after intercourse
Bleeding between periods or after menopause
Unusual vaginal discharge, sometimes foul-smelling
Pelvic pain
Pain during intercourse

body.text: Early cervical cancer may have no symptoms, which is why screening is important.
Stages of Cervical Cancer
Stage 1
Cancer is limited to the cervix.
Stage 2
Cancer has spread beyond the cervix to the upper vagina or tissues beside the uterus, but not to the pelvic wall.
Stage 3
Cancer has spread to the lower vagina, pelvic wall, lymph nodes or causes kidney blockage.
Stage 4
Cancer has spread to the bladder, rectum or distant organs.
Staging uses examination, MRI, CT or PET scans and biopsy results.
Treatment Options by Stage
Very early cancer

items: Cone biopsy or simple hysterectomy
Fertility-sparing surgery (trachelectomy) in selected young women

body.text: Early-stage cancer

items: Radical hysterectomy with lymph node removal
Radiation as an alternative in some cases

body.text: Locally advanced cancer

items: Chemoradiation, often with brachytherapy (internal radiation)

body.text: Advanced or recurrent cancer

items: Chemotherapy
Targeted therapy or immunotherapy in suitable patients
Palliative radiation for symptoms

body.text: Can Fertility Be Preserved?
In some very early cancers, fertility-sparing surgery may be possible. This needs careful assessment by a specialist.
Prevention

items: HPV vaccination: most effective before sexual activity begins
Regular screening: Pap smear and/or HPV test
Avoid smoking: smoking increases risk

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Cervical cancer is mostly caused by HPV.
Early stages are often treated with surgery.
Advanced stages are treated with chemoradiation.
Fertility-sparing options exist for some early cases.
Vaccination and screening prevent many cases.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Cervical cancer is one of the most preventable and treatable cancers when found early. Understanding the stages helps you take part in decisions about your care. For gynecological cancer evaluation, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Can cervical cancer be cured?
faqs.a: Many cervical cancers, especially at early stages, can be cured with surgery or chemoradiation. Outcomes depend on stage, tumour type and overall health.

faqs.q: What is a radical hysterectomy?
faqs.a: It removes the uterus, cervix, part of the vagina and surrounding tissues, often with pelvic lymph nodes. It is used for early-stage cervical cancer.

faqs.q: Is chemoradiation better than surgery?
faqs.a: For early stages, surgery and radiation can be similarly effective. For locally advanced cancer, chemoradiation is usually preferred. Your team will advise based on stage and health.

faqs.q: Can I still have children after cervical cancer?
faqs.a: In some very early cancers, fertility-sparing surgery may allow future pregnancy. This depends on tumour size and stage, and needs specialist evaluation.

faqs.q: Does the HPV vaccine protect against cervical cancer?
faqs.a: Yes. HPV vaccination greatly reduces the risk of cervical cancer, especially when given before exposure to HPV. Screening is still recommended.

faqs.q: What symptoms should never be ignored?
faqs.a: Bleeding after intercourse, bleeding between periods or after menopause and unusual discharge should be checked promptly by a doctor.
