title: Endometrial Cancer: Warning Signs and Surgery
seoTitle: Endometrial Cancer Symptoms | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Endometrial cancer often shows early through abnormal bleeding, especially after menopause. Learn the warning signs, risk factors, tests and how surgery is.
imageAlt: Doctor discussing abnormal bleeding reports with a patient in clinic
quickAnswer: Any bleeding after menopause, heavy or irregular periods after 40 or unusual discharge should be checked. Diagnosis usually involves a transvaginal ultrasound and an endometrial biopsy or hysteroscopy. The main treatment is surgery to remove the uterus, cervix, fallopian tubes and ovaries, often with lymph node assessment. Radiation or other treatments may follow depending on stage.

body.text: Endometrial cancer begins in the lining of the uterus and is the most common cancer of the uterus. Its main early warning sign is abnormal vaginal bleeding, especially any bleeding after menopause. Because this symptom often appears early, many endometrial cancers are found at a stage when surgery alone can be curative.
Warning Signs

items: Bleeding after menopause, even spotting
Heavy, prolonged or irregular periods after 40
Bleeding between periods
Watery or blood-stained discharge
Pelvic pain or pressure in later stages

body.text: Risk Factors

items: Obesity
Diabetes
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
Never having been pregnant
Late menopause
Estrogen therapy without progesterone
Tamoxifen use
Lynch syndrome or family history

body.text: How Is It Diagnosed?

items: Transvaginal ultrasound: measures lining thickness
Endometrial biopsy: a sample of the lining is taken in the clinic
Hysteroscopy: a camera looks inside the uterus and allows targeted biopsy
MRI or CT: to assess spread if cancer is confirmed

body.text: How Is It Treated?
Surgery

items: Total hysterectomy with removal of both ovaries and tubes
Sentinel lymph node mapping or lymph node removal
Often done by laparoscopic or robotic surgery, which may allow faster recovery

body.text: Additional treatment

items: Radiation, including vaginal brachytherapy, for some stages
Chemotherapy for higher-risk or advanced cancers
Hormone therapy in selected cases
Targeted therapy or immunotherapy for some tumour types

body.text: Fertility-sparing treatment
In very early, low-grade cancer in young women, hormone treatment may be considered with close monitoring.
Recovery After Surgery

items: Hospital stay of one to three days after minimally invasive surgery
Return to light activity within two weeks
Avoid heavy lifting and intercourse for about six weeks
Follow-up visits for several years

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Bleeding after menopause is the key warning sign.
Obesity and diabetes increase risk.
Biopsy confirms the diagnosis.
Surgery is the main treatment.
Many cases are found early and cured.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Postmenopausal bleeding should never be ignored. Early evaluation often leads to early diagnosis and very good outcomes. For gynecological cancer assessment and surgery, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Is bleeding after menopause always cancer?
faqs.a: No. It can be caused by thin lining, polyps or hormone changes. However, it should always be checked because it can be the first sign of endometrial cancer.

faqs.q: Can endometrial cancer be treated with laparoscopic surgery?
faqs.a: Yes. Many patients are treated with laparoscopic or robotic hysterectomy, which may mean less pain and quicker recovery than open surgery.

faqs.q: Do both ovaries need to be removed?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes, as part of standard surgery. In some younger women with very early cancer, ovary preservation may be discussed.

faqs.q: Will I need radiation after surgery?
faqs.a: It depends on stage, grade and other features. Some women need no further treatment, while others benefit from radiation or chemotherapy.

faqs.q: Does obesity increase endometrial cancer risk?
faqs.a: Yes. Excess body fat raises estrogen levels, which can stimulate the uterine lining. Maintaining a healthy weight lowers risk.

faqs.q: Is endometrial cancer hereditary?
faqs.a: Most cases are not inherited, but Lynch syndrome raises risk. Women with a strong family history of uterine or colon cancer may benefit from genetic counselling.

title: Radical Hysterectomy: What It Involves and Recovery
seoTitle: Radical Hysterectomy | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Radical hysterectomy removes the uterus, cervix, surrounding tissue and upper vagina to treat early cervical cancer. Learn how it differs from simple.
imageAlt: Surgeon explaining radical hysterectomy on a pelvic anatomy model
quickAnswer: Radical hysterectomy is done to remove cancer with a wide margin of healthy tissue. It may be open or minimally invasive, depending on the case and current evidence. Hospital stay is often several days. Recovery usually takes six to eight weeks. Some women may have temporary bladder problems because of nerves near the operated area.

body.text: A radical hysterectomy is surgery that removes the uterus, cervix, the tissues beside the uterus (parametrium) and the upper part of the vagina. Pelvic lymph nodes are usually removed too. It is mainly used for early-stage cervical cancer and some other gynecological cancers. It is more extensive than a simple hysterectomy, which removes only the uterus and cervix.
Simple vs Radical Hysterectomy
Simple hysterectomy
Removes the uterus and cervix.
Radical hysterectomy
Removes the uterus, cervix, parametrium, upper vagina and usually pelvic lymph nodes.
Ovaries
Ovaries may or may not be removed, depending on age, cancer type and risk. Younger women may keep their ovaries to avoid early menopause.
Who Needs It?

items: Early-stage cervical cancer
Some endometrial cancers involving the cervix
Selected other gynecological cancers

body.text: Surgical Approaches

items: Open surgery: through an abdominal incision
Laparoscopic or robotic surgery: through small cuts

body.text: For cervical cancer, many centres now prefer open radical hysterectomy based on research findings. Your surgeon will explain the safest approach for your situation.
What Happens After Surgery?

items: Hospital stay of several days
A urinary catheter for some days, sometimes longer
Pain relief and early walking
Gradual return to eating and activity

body.text: Possible Side Effects

items: Temporary difficulty emptying the bladder
Constipation
Lymphedema of the legs if lymph nodes are removed
Shortening of the vagina, which may affect intercourse
Early menopause if ovaries are removed

body.text: Recovery at Home

items: Avoid heavy lifting for about six weeks
Avoid intercourse until your doctor confirms healing
Walk daily to support recovery
Watch for fever, heavy bleeding, wound problems or leg swelling

body.text: Will I Need Further Treatment?
Depending on final pathology, some women need radiation or chemoradiation after surgery.
Key Takeaways

items: Radical hysterectomy is more extensive than simple hysterectomy.
It is mainly used for early cervical cancer.
Pelvic lymph nodes are often removed.
Temporary bladder issues are possible.
Recovery usually takes six to eight weeks.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Knowing what radical hysterectomy involves helps you prepare and recover with confidence. Open discussion with your team about every question is encouraged. For gynecological cancer surgery, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: How long is the hospital stay after radical hysterectomy?
faqs.a: Most women stay in hospital for several days. The stay depends on the surgical approach, bladder recovery and overall health.

faqs.q: Will I go into menopause after radical hysterectomy?
faqs.a: Only if the ovaries are removed. In younger women with early cervical cancer, ovaries are often preserved to avoid early menopause.

faqs.q: Why do some women need a catheter for longer?
faqs.a: Nerves controlling the bladder lie near the surgical area. Surgery can temporarily affect bladder emptying, so a catheter may be needed until function returns.

faqs.q: Can I have a normal sex life after radical hysterectomy?
faqs.a: Many women do. The vagina may be shorter, and some may have dryness or discomfort. Lubricants, gradual resumption and talking to your doctor help.

faqs.q: Is laparoscopic radical hysterectomy safe?
faqs.a: For cervical cancer, research has led many centres to prefer open surgery. For other conditions, minimally invasive surgery may be suitable. Your surgeon will discuss the evidence.

faqs.q: Will I need radiation after surgery?
faqs.a: Some women do, depending on lymph nodes, margins and tumour features found after surgery. Your team will plan this after reviewing pathology.

title: Postmenopausal Bleeding: When Is It a Warning Sign?
seoTitle: Postmenopausal Bleeding Causes | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Any vaginal bleeding after menopause needs medical attention. Learn the common causes, why cancer must be ruled out and which tests doctors use to find the.
imageAlt: Woman consulting a doctor about postmenopausal bleeding in a clinic
quickAnswer: Even light spotting or pink discharge after menopause needs evaluation. Common causes include vaginal atrophy, endometrial atrophy, polyps and hormone therapy, but endometrial hyperplasia or cancer must be ruled out. Doctors usually use a transvaginal ultrasound and, if needed, an endometrial biopsy or hysteroscopy.

body.text: Postmenopausal bleeding is any vaginal bleeding that happens 12 months or more after a woman's last period. It should always be checked by a doctor. Most cases are caused by harmless conditions like thinning of the vaginal or uterine lining, but it can also be the first sign of endometrial cancer, so prompt evaluation is important.
Common Causes
Non-cancerous causes

items: Thinning of the vaginal lining (vaginal atrophy)
Thinning of the uterine lining (endometrial atrophy)
Endometrial or cervical polyps
Hormone replacement therapy
Infections
Blood-thinning medicines

body.text: Pre-cancerous and cancerous causes

items: Endometrial hyperplasia (thickening of the lining)
Endometrial cancer
Cervical cancer
Rarely, ovarian or vaginal cancers

body.text: Why Should It Never Be Ignored?
Bleeding after menopause is the most common symptom of endometrial cancer. When checked early, many cancers are found at an early stage, when treatment is most successful.
How Is It Evaluated?
History and examination
Your doctor asks about bleeding pattern, medicines and health conditions, and examines the vagina and cervix.
Transvaginal ultrasound
Measures endometrial thickness. A thin lining usually suggests a benign cause.
Endometrial biopsy
A small sample of the lining is taken, often in the clinic.
Hysteroscopy
A thin camera looks inside the uterus to find polyps or abnormal areas and take biopsies.
Pap smear or HPV test
To check the cervix.
Who Is at Higher Risk of Cancer?

items: Obesity
Diabetes
High blood pressure
Estrogen-only hormone therapy
Tamoxifen use
Family history or Lynch syndrome

body.text: What Happens Next?

items: Atrophy may be treated with vaginal moisturisers or local hormone creams
Polyps can be removed during hysteroscopy
Hyperplasia may be treated with hormones or surgery
Cancer is usually treated with surgery and sometimes additional therapy

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Any bleeding after menopause needs checking.
Most causes are not cancer.
Endometrial cancer must be ruled out.
Ultrasound and biopsy are key tests.
Early evaluation leads to better outcomes.

body.text: Final Thoughts

It is easy to dismiss a small amount of bleeding, but it is your body's signal to get checked. Early evaluation brings either reassurance or early treatment. For assessment of postmenopausal bleeding, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Is spotting after menopause normal?
faqs.a: No. Any bleeding or spotting after 12 months without a period should be evaluated. Most causes are harmless, but cancer must be ruled out.

faqs.q: What is the most common cause of postmenopausal bleeding?
faqs.a: Thinning of the vaginal or uterine lining due to low estrogen is the most common cause. Polyps and hormone therapy are also common.

faqs.q: What does a thick endometrium mean?
faqs.a: A thickened lining on ultrasound may suggest hyperplasia, polyps or cancer and usually needs a biopsy. A thin lining is often reassuring.

faqs.q: Is an endometrial biopsy painful?
faqs.a: It may cause cramping similar to period pain for a short time. Pain relief before the procedure can help. It is usually done quickly in the clinic.

faqs.q: Can hormone therapy cause bleeding after menopause?
faqs.a: Yes. Some hormone therapies cause bleeding, especially at the start. Unexpected or persistent bleeding should still be checked.

faqs.q: How soon should I see a doctor?
faqs.a: As soon as possible, ideally within a couple of weeks. Do not wait for it to happen again before getting evaluated.

title: Mouth Cancer Early Signs You Should Not Ignore
seoTitle: Mouth Cancer Symptoms | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Mouth cancer often starts as a non-healing ulcer or white or red patch. Learn the early signs, high-risk habits and why any mouth sore lasting more than two.
imageAlt: Doctor examining a patient mouth with a light in a clinic
quickAnswer: See a doctor if you have a mouth sore, ulcer, white patch (leukoplakia), red patch (erythroplakia), lump or rough area that lasts more than two weeks, especially if you use tobacco, gutka, paan or alcohol. A biopsy confirms the diagnosis. Early treatment with surgery often gives excellent results.

body.text: Mouth (oral) cancer is one of the most common cancers in India, largely due to tobacco and areca nut use. Early signs include a mouth ulcer that does not heal within two to three weeks, white or red patches, a lump or thickening in the cheek, and difficulty opening the mouth. Found early, mouth cancer is highly treatable.
Early Warning Signs

items: Ulcer or sore in the mouth that does not heal in two to three weeks
White or red patches on the gums, tongue, cheeks or palate
A lump or thickening in the cheek, tongue or gums
Pain or burning that does not go away
Difficulty opening the mouth fully (trismus)
Loose teeth without gum disease
Dentures that suddenly do not fit
Bleeding from the mouth
Numbness in the tongue or lips
A lump in the neck

body.text: Pre-Cancerous Conditions

items: Leukoplakia: white patch that cannot be wiped off
Erythroplakia: red patch, higher risk of cancer
Oral submucous fibrosis: stiffening of the mouth lining, often from areca nut use, causing reduced mouth opening

body.text: These need regular monitoring or treatment.
Who Is at Higher Risk?

items: Tobacco smokers and chewers
Users of gutka, paan, areca nut or khaini
Heavy alcohol users
Poor oral hygiene
Sharp teeth or ill-fitting dentures causing chronic irritation
HPV infection for some throat cancers

body.text: How Is It Diagnosed?

items: Clinical examination of the mouth and neck
Biopsy of the suspicious area
Imaging such as CT, MRI or PET-CT to check spread

body.text: How Is It Treated?

items: Surgery: main treatment for most mouth cancers, removing the tumour with margins and often neck lymph nodes
Reconstruction: to restore appearance and function
Radiation or chemoradiation: after surgery in some cases

body.text: How Can You Reduce Risk?

items: Stop all tobacco and areca nut use
Limit alcohol
Maintain good oral hygiene
Get dental problems fixed
Do monthly self-checks of your mouth

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Mouth cancer is common in India.
Non-healing ulcers and patches are early signs.
Tobacco and areca nut are major causes.
Any sore lasting two weeks needs checking.
Early surgery gives good outcomes.

body.text: Final Thoughts

A small sore that does not heal may be your body's early warning. Acting quickly can save your life and preserve function. For head and neck cancer evaluation, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: What does early mouth cancer look like?
faqs.a: It may look like a small ulcer, white or red patch, or rough area that does not heal. It may be painless at first. Any such change lasting over two weeks should be checked.

faqs.q: Can mouth ulcers be cancer?
faqs.a: Most mouth ulcers are harmless and heal within two weeks. Ulcers that persist, grow or bleed may be cancer and need a biopsy.

faqs.q: Is gutka more dangerous than smoking?
faqs.a: Both are harmful. Chewing tobacco, gutka and areca nut are strongly linked to mouth cancer in India. Stopping any form of tobacco reduces risk.

faqs.q: Can mouth cancer be cured?
faqs.a: Yes, especially when found early. Surgery, sometimes with radiation, can cure many early mouth cancers. Outcomes are best with early diagnosis.

faqs.q: What is oral submucous fibrosis?
faqs.a: It is a condition where the mouth lining stiffens, often due to areca nut chewing, making it hard to open the mouth. It increases the risk of mouth cancer.

faqs.q: How can I check my mouth at home?
faqs.a: Use a mirror and good light to look at your lips, gums, cheeks, tongue and palate monthly. Feel for lumps. Report anything unusual lasting more than two weeks.

title: Tobacco, Gutka and Head and Neck Cancer Risk
seoTitle: Gutka and Oral Cancer | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Tobacco in any form, including gutka, khaini and areca nut, sharply raises head and neck cancer risk. Learn how it damages tissue, warning signs.

about.n: Oral cancer risk from tobacco and areca nut

imageAlt: Man throwing away a tobacco packet into a street dustbin
quickAnswer: Tobacco contains many cancer-causing chemicals that damage cells in the mouth and throat. Smokeless tobacco held in the mouth for long periods is especially linked to mouth cancer. Combining tobacco with alcohol multiplies the risk. Stopping tobacco reduces cancer risk progressively, and support is available to help people quit.

body.text: Tobacco use is the leading cause of head and neck cancers in India, including cancers of the mouth, tongue, throat and voice box. Both smoking and smokeless forms, such as gutka, khaini, zarda, paan with tobacco and mawa, damage the lining of the mouth and throat. Areca nut (supari) on its own is also linked to cancer. Quitting at any age lowers the risk over time.
Forms of Tobacco Linked to Cancer
Smoked

items: Cigarettes
Bidis
Hookah

body.text: Smokeless

items: Gutka
Khaini
Zarda
Mawa
Paan with tobacco
Snuff and mishri

body.text: Areca nut
Supari is classified as a cancer-causing substance and is linked to oral submucous fibrosis and mouth cancer.
How Does Tobacco Cause Cancer?

items: Chemicals damage the DNA of cells lining the mouth and throat
Constant irritation leads to pre-cancerous changes
Smokeless tobacco kept against the cheek causes long contact with tissue
Alcohol helps chemicals penetrate tissues more easily

body.text: Which Cancers Are Linked?

items: Mouth, including cheek, gums and tongue
Throat (pharynx)
Voice box (larynx)
Food pipe (esophagus)
Lip and nasal sinuses in some cases

body.text: Warning Signs in Tobacco Users

items: Non-healing mouth ulcers
White or red patches
Reduced mouth opening
Persistent hoarseness of voice
Difficulty swallowing
Neck lump
Ear pain without ear infection

body.text: Benefits of Quitting

items: Mouth lining begins to heal
Pre-cancerous patches may improve
Cancer risk falls over the years
Better gum and dental health
Improved outcomes if cancer treatment is needed

body.text: How to Quit

items: Set a quit date and tell family
Remove tobacco products from home and work
Identify triggers such as tea, stress or after meals
Use nicotine replacement therapy if advised by a doctor
Seek counselling or quitline support
Replace the habit with healthy alternatives like fennel seeds or sugar-free gum

body.text: India's national tobacco quitline offers free support. Your doctor can share the current number.
Key Takeaways

items: Tobacco is the main cause of head and neck cancer in India.
Smokeless tobacco and areca nut are also harmful.
Alcohol multiplies the risk.
Warning signs should be checked early.
Quitting lowers risk at any age.

body.text: Final Thoughts

It is never too late to stop tobacco. Every day without it is a step toward better health. If you notice warning signs, get checked early. For head and neck cancer screening and treatment, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Is smokeless tobacco safer than smoking?
faqs.a: No. Smokeless tobacco like gutka and khaini is strongly linked to mouth cancer. All forms of tobacco are harmful.

faqs.q: Does areca nut alone cause cancer?
faqs.a: Yes. Areca nut is considered cancer-causing and is linked to oral submucous fibrosis and mouth cancer, even without tobacco.

faqs.q: How long after quitting does cancer risk drop?
faqs.a: Risk starts falling soon after quitting and continues to decrease over years. The longer you stay tobacco-free, the greater the benefit.

faqs.q: Does drinking alcohol increase the risk?
faqs.a: Yes. Alcohol combined with tobacco greatly multiplies the risk of head and neck cancers. Reducing or avoiding both is best.

faqs.q: Can pre-cancerous patches go away after quitting?
faqs.a: Some white patches may shrink or disappear after stopping tobacco. They still need monitoring by a doctor, and some may need treatment.

faqs.q: What help is available to quit tobacco?
faqs.a: Counselling, nicotine replacement therapy, medicines prescribed by a doctor and national quitline services can help. Combining support methods improves success.

title: Thyroid Cancer Surgery: Types and Recovery
seoTitle: Thyroid Cancer Surgery | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Thyroid cancer is often treated with surgery to remove part or all of the thyroid. Learn about lobectomy vs total thyroidectomy, risks to voice and calcium.
imageAlt: Young woman viewing a small healing neck scar after thyroid surgery
quickAnswer: Small, low-risk thyroid cancers may be treated with lobectomy. Larger tumours, cancers in both lobes, spread to lymph nodes or higher-risk features often need total thyroidectomy. After total thyroidectomy, lifelong thyroid hormone tablets are needed. Radioactive iodine may be advised in some cases. Key surgical risks are voice changes and low calcium, which are usually temporary.

body.text: Surgery is the main treatment for most thyroid cancers. Depending on tumour size, type and spread, the surgeon may remove one lobe of the thyroid (lobectomy) or the whole gland (total thyroidectomy). Nearby lymph nodes may also be removed. Most people recover well and return to normal activities within one to two weeks.
Types of Thyroid Cancer

items: Papillary: most common, usually slow-growing
Follicular: also usually treatable
Medullary: may be hereditary
Anaplastic: rare and aggressive

body.text: Types of Surgery
Lobectomy (hemithyroidectomy)
Removes one half of the thyroid. Some people keep enough function to avoid hormone tablets.
Total thyroidectomy
Removes the entire thyroid. Thyroid hormone replacement is needed for life.
Neck dissection
Removes lymph nodes in the central or side of the neck if cancer has spread or is suspected.
How Is It Decided?

items: Tumour size and type
Whether one or both lobes are involved
Lymph node spread
Biopsy and ultrasound findings
Patient preference after discussion

body.text: Possible Risks

items: Voice changes: from irritation or injury to the nerve that controls the vocal cords, usually temporary
Low calcium: if parathyroid glands are affected, causing tingling or cramps, usually temporary
Bleeding or swelling in the neck: rare but needs urgent attention
Scar: usually small and fades over time

body.text: Recovery

items: Hospital stay of one to two days
Mild neck pain and swallowing discomfort for a few days
Calcium levels checked after surgery
Return to work in about one to two weeks
Avoid heavy lifting for about two weeks

body.text: After Surgery

items: Thyroid hormone tablets if needed
Radioactive iodine for some patients
Regular blood tests (thyroid levels and thyroglobulin) and ultrasound follow-up

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Surgery is the main treatment for thyroid cancer.
Lobectomy or total thyroidectomy depends on risk.
Voice and calcium problems are usually temporary.
Hormone tablets are needed after total removal.
Most people recover within a couple of weeks.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Most thyroid cancers have excellent outcomes with timely surgery and follow-up. Knowing what to expect helps you feel ready. For thyroid cancer surgery evaluation, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Will I need thyroid tablets after surgery?
faqs.a: After total thyroidectomy, yes, for life. After lobectomy, some people need tablets and others do not, depending on thyroid function tests.

faqs.q: Can thyroid surgery affect my voice?
faqs.a: Temporary hoarseness is fairly common and usually improves within weeks. Permanent voice change is uncommon with experienced surgeons.

faqs.q: Why is calcium checked after thyroid surgery?
faqs.a: The parathyroid glands, which control calcium, sit close to the thyroid. They may be affected during surgery, causing temporary low calcium.

faqs.q: Is radioactive iodine always needed?
faqs.a: No. It is used for some patients with higher-risk features or spread. Many low-risk patients do not need it.

faqs.q: How big is the scar after thyroid surgery?
faqs.a: The scar is usually a few centimetres long and placed in a natural skin crease. It typically fades well over months.

faqs.q: Is thyroid cancer curable?
faqs.a: Most thyroid cancers, especially papillary and follicular types, have excellent cure rates with surgery and appropriate follow-up treatment.

title: Neck Dissection: Why Lymph Nodes Are Removed
seoTitle: Neck Dissection | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Neck dissection removes lymph nodes in the neck to treat or prevent cancer spread. Learn the types, why it is done, possible effects on shoulder movement.
imageAlt: Patient doing shoulder rotation exercises with a physiotherapist
quickAnswer: Neck dissection is done to treat cancer that has spread to neck nodes (therapeutic) or to remove nodes at high risk of hidden spread (elective). It helps with staging and guides further treatment such as radiation. Types range from selective dissection, which removes certain node groups, to more extensive dissection. Recovery usually takes a few weeks, with physiotherapy for shoulder movement.

body.text: A neck dissection is surgery to remove lymph nodes and surrounding tissue from the neck. It is commonly done for head and neck cancers, such as mouth, throat, voice box and thyroid cancer, because these cancers often spread to neck lymph nodes first. It may be done to remove known cancer spread or to remove nodes that might contain hidden cancer cells.
Why Is It Done?

items: To remove lymph nodes with known cancer
To remove nodes that may contain microscopic cancer
To stage the cancer accurately
To decide whether radiation or chemotherapy is needed

body.text: Types of Neck Dissection
Selective neck dissection
Removes specific groups of lymph nodes most at risk. Important nerves, muscles and veins are preserved.
Modified radical neck dissection
Removes all lymph node groups on one side, preserving one or more important structures.
Radical neck dissection
Removes all lymph nodes plus certain muscles, a major vein and a nerve. Used less often today, mainly for extensive disease.
Possible Effects

items: Shoulder stiffness or weakness: if the nerve to the shoulder muscle is affected
Numbness: of the neck, ear or skin around the scar
Swelling: of the face or neck, usually temporary
Fluid collection or chyle leak: uncommon
Scar: along the neck crease

body.text: Recovery

items: Hospital stay of a few days, often combined with the main tumour surgery
Drains removed within several days
Gentle neck and shoulder exercises begin early
Physiotherapy helps restore shoulder movement
Return to light activities within a few weeks

body.text: What Happens After?
The pathologist examines the nodes. If cancer is found in many nodes or spread outside the node, radiation or chemoradiation may be recommended.
Key Takeaways

items: Neck dissection removes lymph nodes in the neck.
It treats or prevents cancer spread.
Selective dissection preserves key structures.
Shoulder stiffness can occur and improves with physiotherapy.
Results guide further treatment.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Neck dissection is an important part of head and neck cancer care that helps control disease and plan treatment. Physiotherapy and follow-up support a smooth recovery. For head and neck cancer surgery, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Why are lymph nodes removed in head and neck cancer?
faqs.a: These cancers often spread first to neck nodes. Removing them helps treat existing spread, find hidden cancer and plan further treatment.

faqs.q: Will neck dissection affect my shoulder?
faqs.a: Some people develop shoulder stiffness or weakness, especially if the accessory nerve is affected. Physiotherapy usually improves movement.

faqs.q: How long is recovery after neck dissection?
faqs.a: Most people recover over a few weeks. Neck and shoulder exercises continue for longer to restore full movement.

faqs.q: Is numbness after neck dissection permanent?
faqs.a: Numbness around the neck and ear is common. It often improves over months, though some areas may stay numb.

faqs.q: Do all patients with mouth cancer need neck dissection?
faqs.a: Many do, as nodes may contain hidden cancer. The decision depends on tumour size, depth and location. Your surgeon will advise.

faqs.q: Will I need radiation after neck dissection?
faqs.a: It depends on the pathology report. Radiation may be advised if several nodes contain cancer or other high-risk features are present.

title: Speech and Swallowing After Head and Neck Surgery
seoTitle: Swallowing After Head and Neck Surgery | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Head and neck cancer surgery can affect speech and swallowing. Learn why changes happen, how speech and swallow therapy helps and what to expect during.
primaryKeyword: swallowing after head and neck surgery

about.n: Dysphagia after head and neck surgery

imageAlt: Therapist guiding a patient through swallowing exercises in rehabilitation
quickAnswer: Speech and swallowing may change because muscles, nerves or tissues involved in these functions are removed or reconstructed. A speech and swallowing therapist assesses your ability, teaches exercises and safe swallowing techniques, and adjusts food textures. Some people need a temporary feeding tube. Starting therapy early improves recovery.

body.text: Surgery for cancers of the mouth, tongue, throat or voice box can affect how you speak and swallow. Changes depend on which area is treated, how much tissue is removed and whether radiation follows. With speech and swallowing therapy, most people improve significantly over weeks to months and return to eating and communicating comfortably.
Why Do Changes Happen?

items: Removal of part of the tongue, palate, jaw or throat
Swelling after surgery
Nerve changes affecting muscle control
Reconstruction with tissue flaps that move differently
Radiation causing stiffness and dryness
Tracheostomy affecting airflow for speech

body.text: Common Speech Changes

items: Slurred or unclear words
Nasal-sounding voice
Hoarseness
Reduced loudness
Difficulty with certain sounds

body.text: Common Swallowing Changes

items: Difficulty moving food in the mouth
Food sticking in the throat
Coughing or choking while eating
Food or liquid going into the airway (aspiration)
Dry mouth after radiation

body.text: How Does Therapy Help?
Assessment
A speech and swallowing therapist checks muscle strength, movement and swallowing safety. Tests such as video fluoroscopy or endoscopic swallow studies may be used.
Exercises
Tongue, jaw, lip and throat exercises strengthen muscles and improve range of motion.
Swallowing strategies
Head positions, small bites, double swallows and slow eating improve safety.
Diet changes
Food textures may start as liquids or purees and progress to soft and regular foods.
Speech practice
Exercises improve clarity and voice strength.
Feeding Tubes
Some people need a temporary nasogastric tube or a feeding tube in the stomach to maintain nutrition while healing. Most can return to oral eating as swallowing improves.
Living With Changes

items: Practise exercises daily
Keep the mouth moist with water and saliva substitutes
Maintain oral hygiene
Eat in a calm environment
Join support groups if available

body.text: When to Seek Help

items: Frequent coughing or choking during meals
Chest infections or fever
Weight loss
Difficulty being understood

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Surgery can affect speech and swallowing.
Changes depend on the area treated.
Therapy improves function significantly.
Diet textures may need adjustment.
Early rehabilitation gives the best results.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Speech and swallowing changes can feel overwhelming at first, but steady therapy brings real progress. You are not alone in this recovery. For head and neck cancer surgery and rehabilitation planning, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Will I be able to speak normally after tongue surgery?
faqs.a: Many people regain clear speech, especially after partial tongue removal with good reconstruction. Speech therapy plays a major role in improvement.

faqs.q: How long will I need a feeding tube?
faqs.a: It varies. Some people need it for days or weeks, others longer, especially with radiation. It is removed when you can eat safely and maintain weight.

faqs.q: Why do I cough when swallowing?
faqs.a: Coughing may mean food or liquid is entering the airway. A swallowing assessment helps find safe techniques and textures to prevent this.

faqs.q: Can radiation make swallowing worse?
faqs.a: Yes. Radiation can cause stiffness, dryness and swelling. Continuing swallowing exercises during and after radiation helps maintain function.

faqs.q: When should swallowing therapy start?
faqs.a: Ideally before or soon after surgery. Early therapy helps prevent stiffness and supports faster recovery.

faqs.q: Can I eat normal food again?
faqs.a: Many people return to most foods over time, sometimes with modifications. A therapist and dietitian help you progress safely.

title: What Is Peritoneal Metastasis?
seoTitle: Peritoneal Metastasis | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Peritoneal metastasis is cancer spread to the lining of the abdomen. Learn which cancers cause it, common symptoms, how it is diagnosed and when CRS.
imageAlt: Oncologist explaining an abdominal CT scan to a concerned couple
quickAnswer: Peritoneal metastasis means tumour deposits on the abdominal lining. Symptoms may include bloating, abdominal swelling from fluid (ascites), pain, early fullness and bowel changes. Diagnosis uses CT, MRI or PET scans and often laparoscopy. Treatment may include chemotherapy, and in suitable patients, CRS and HIPEC.

body.text: Peritoneal metastasis is when cancer spreads to the peritoneum, the thin lining that covers the inside of the abdomen and the organs within it. It most often comes from cancers of the ovary, colon, rectum, stomach, appendix or pancreas. It was once considered untreatable, but for selected patients, cytoreductive surgery (CRS) with HIPEC can offer long-term control.
What Is the Peritoneum?
It is a smooth, thin membrane that lines the abdominal wall and covers organs like the stomach, intestines and liver. It produces a small amount of fluid that allows organs to move smoothly.
Which Cancers Spread to the Peritoneum?

items: Ovarian cancer
Colorectal cancer
Appendix cancer, including pseudomyxoma peritonei
Stomach cancer
Pancreatic cancer
Primary peritoneal cancer
Peritoneal mesothelioma

body.text: Common Symptoms

items: Bloating or abdominal swelling
Fluid in the abdomen (ascites)
Abdominal pain or discomfort
Feeling full quickly
Nausea or vomiting
Change in bowel habits
Unexplained weight loss
Signs of bowel blockage in advanced cases

body.text: How Is It Diagnosed?

items: CT scan: often the first test
MRI or PET-CT: for more detail
Tumour markers: such as CEA or CA-125
Fluid analysis: if ascites is present
Diagnostic laparoscopy: to look directly at the extent of spread and take biopsies

body.text: What Is the PCI Score?
The Peritoneal Cancer Index scores how much cancer is present in different parts of the abdomen. It helps decide whether CRS and HIPEC are suitable.
How Is It Treated?
Systemic chemotherapy
Given through the vein to control cancer throughout the body.
Cytoreductive surgery (CRS)
Surgery to remove all visible tumour from the abdomen.
HIPEC
Heated chemotherapy washed through the abdomen after CRS to target remaining microscopic cancer cells.
PIPAC
A newer technique delivering aerosolised chemotherapy in selected patients.
Palliative care
To manage symptoms such as fluid build-up or bowel blockage.
Who May Benefit From CRS and HIPEC?
Patients with limited, removable peritoneal disease, good general health and no widespread spread to other organs.
Key Takeaways

items: Peritoneal metastasis is spread to the abdominal lining.
It often comes from ovarian, colorectal or appendix cancer.
Bloating and ascites are common symptoms.
Laparoscopy and PCI help guide treatment.
CRS and HIPEC may help selected patients.

body.text: Final Thoughts

A diagnosis of peritoneal spread is serious, but it no longer always means there are no options. Specialist evaluation can open the door to treatment. For peritoneal surface oncology assessment, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Is peritoneal metastasis stage 4 cancer?
faqs.a: Often yes, as it represents spread beyond the original organ. However, some patients with limited peritoneal spread can still be treated with curative intent.

faqs.q: Can peritoneal metastasis be cured?
faqs.a: In selected patients, especially with limited disease from appendix, colorectal or ovarian cancer, CRS and HIPEC can offer long-term survival. Outcomes depend on many factors.

faqs.q: What causes fluid in the abdomen with cancer?
faqs.a: Cancer cells on the peritoneum can cause fluid production and block drainage, leading to ascites. It may be drained for comfort.

faqs.q: How is peritoneal spread detected?
faqs.a: CT, MRI or PET scans are used first. Small deposits may not show on scans, so diagnostic laparoscopy is often needed.

faqs.q: What is the PCI score?
faqs.a: It is a score from 0 to 39 that measures how widespread cancer is in the abdomen. Lower scores generally mean better chances with surgery.

faqs.q: Is chemotherapy alone enough?
faqs.a: For some patients, chemotherapy is the main treatment. For others with limited disease, combining surgery and HIPEC may give better results.

title: Who Is a Candidate for CRS and HIPEC?
seoTitle: Who Is a Candidate for CRS and HIPEC | Dr Varadharajan V
description: CRS and HIPEC can help selected patients with cancer spread to the abdominal lining. Learn the key criteria, which cancers respond best and why careful.
imageAlt: Cancer specialists discussing scans around a conference table
quickAnswer: CRS and HIPEC may be considered for patients with peritoneal spread from appendix cancer, pseudomyxoma peritonei, colorectal cancer, ovarian cancer, peritoneal mesothelioma and selected stomach cancers. Key requirements include no widespread spread outside the abdomen, a manageable PCI score, the ability to remove all visible tumour, and fitness for major surgery.

body.text: Cytoreductive surgery (CRS) with hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) is a specialised treatment for cancer that has spread to the lining of the abdomen. It is not suitable for everyone. The best candidates have cancer limited mainly to the abdomen, disease that can be completely removed, good overall health and a cancer type known to respond to this approach.
Cancers That May Benefit

items: Pseudomyxoma peritonei
Appendix cancers
Colorectal cancer with limited peritoneal spread
Ovarian cancer, especially in selected stages
Peritoneal mesothelioma
Selected stomach cancers in specialised centres

body.text: Key Selection Criteria
Disease limited to the abdomen
No significant spread to the lungs, bones, brain or many liver sites.
PCI score
The Peritoneal Cancer Index measures the amount of disease. Lower scores are associated with better outcomes. Acceptable limits vary by cancer type.
Complete cytoreduction possible
The surgeon must be able to remove all visible tumour. Incomplete removal reduces benefit.
Good general health
Heart, lung, kidney and liver function must be strong enough for long surgery.
Response to chemotherapy
For some cancers, response to systemic chemotherapy helps predict benefit.
Patient motivation and support
Recovery is demanding, so commitment and family support matter.
How Is Suitability Assessed?

items: CT, MRI or PET-CT scans
Tumour markers
Diagnostic laparoscopy to directly assess spread
Fitness tests
Discussion at a tumour board

body.text: Who Is Usually Not Suitable?

items: Widespread cancer outside the abdomen
Very high PCI scores for certain cancers
Extensive small bowel involvement
Poor general health or frailty
Cancer that is progressing rapidly despite chemotherapy

body.text: Why Experience Matters
CRS and HIPEC are complex procedures. Outcomes are better in centres with experienced surgical, anaesthesia and critical care teams.
Key Takeaways

items: CRS and HIPEC are for selected patients.
Disease must be mainly within the abdomen.
Complete removal of visible tumour is essential.
PCI score guides decisions.
Experienced centres improve outcomes.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Careful selection is the key to safe and effective CRS and HIPEC. A detailed evaluation helps decide whether this treatment can offer you real benefit. For CRS and HIPEC assessment, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Which cancers respond best to CRS and HIPEC?
faqs.a: Pseudomyxoma peritonei and appendix cancers often respond very well. Colorectal and ovarian cancers with limited spread can also benefit in selected patients.

faqs.q: What PCI score is acceptable for HIPEC?
faqs.a: It depends on the cancer type. Lower scores generally mean better outcomes. Your surgeon will interpret your score in the context of your cancer.

faqs.q: Can elderly patients have CRS and HIPEC?
faqs.a: Age alone is not a barrier, but overall fitness matters. Older patients with good health may still be considered after careful assessment.

faqs.q: Do I need chemotherapy before HIPEC?
faqs.a: Many patients receive systemic chemotherapy before surgery to shrink disease and test response. The plan depends on cancer type and stage.

faqs.q: Why is diagnostic laparoscopy done before CRS?
faqs.a: Scans can underestimate peritoneal disease. Laparoscopy allows direct viewing to confirm whether complete removal is possible.

faqs.q: Is CRS and HIPEC a cure?
faqs.a: For some patients, it offers long-term survival and possible cure. For others, it extends life and controls disease. Outcomes vary by cancer type and extent.

title: What Is the PCI Score in Peritoneal Cancer?
seoTitle: What Is the PCI Score | Dr Varadharajan V
description: The Peritoneal Cancer Index (PCI) scores how much cancer has spread in the abdomen. Learn how it is calculated, what the numbers mean and how it guides CRS.
imageAlt: Surgeon sketching an abdominal grid to explain the PCI score
quickAnswer: A lower PCI means less cancer spread and usually a better chance of complete removal and good outcomes. A higher PCI means more widespread disease. The acceptable PCI for surgery depends on the cancer type. For example, pseudomyxoma peritonei may be treated even at higher scores, while colorectal or stomach cancers usually need lower scores.

body.text: The Peritoneal Cancer Index (PCI) is a scoring system that measures how much cancer has spread across the lining of the abdomen. Surgeons divide the abdomen into 13 regions and score the size of tumour deposits in each from 0 to 3. The total ranges from 0 to 39. The PCI helps decide whether cytoreductive surgery and HIPEC are likely to help.
How Is the PCI Calculated?
13 regions
The abdomen is divided into:

items: 9 regions in a grid covering the abdomen
4 regions covering parts of the small intestine

body.text: Lesion size score
Each region is scored:

items: 0: no visible tumour
1: tumour up to 0.5 cm
2: tumour from 0.5 to 5 cm
3: tumour larger than 5 cm or merging deposits

body.text: The scores are added to give the total PCI.
How Is PCI Measured?

items: Imaging: CT, MRI or PET-CT can estimate PCI but may underestimate small deposits
Diagnostic laparoscopy: allows direct viewing and more accurate scoring
During surgery: the final PCI is recorded at the time of operation

body.text: Why Does PCI Matter?

items: Predicts whether complete removal is possible
Helps estimate outcomes
Guides decisions about surgery versus chemotherapy
Allows comparison over time and between treatments

body.text: PCI and Different Cancers

items: Pseudomyxoma peritonei: may be treated even with high PCI
Colorectal cancer: lower PCI scores are generally preferred for benefit
Ovarian cancer: decisions depend on PCI and the ability to remove all disease
Stomach cancer: usually only very low PCI is considered

body.text: Exact thresholds vary between guidelines and centres.
Other Factors Besides PCI

items: Small bowel involvement
Spread outside the abdomen
Patient fitness
Response to chemotherapy
Tumour biology

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: PCI measures peritoneal cancer spread.
It ranges from 0 to 39.
Lower scores usually mean better outcomes.
Acceptable scores vary by cancer type.
Laparoscopy gives more accurate scoring.

body.text: Final Thoughts

The PCI score is one important tool, but decisions are always based on the full clinical picture. Understanding it helps you follow treatment discussions with confidence. For CRS and HIPEC evaluation, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: What is a good PCI score?
faqs.a: Lower scores are generally better. What counts as acceptable depends on the cancer type. Your surgeon will explain what your score means in your situation.

faqs.q: Can a CT scan give an accurate PCI?
faqs.a: CT can estimate PCI but often underestimates small deposits. Diagnostic laparoscopy or findings during surgery provide a more accurate score.

faqs.q: Does a high PCI mean surgery is not possible?
faqs.a: Not always. For some cancers like pseudomyxoma peritonei, surgery may still be possible with high scores. For others, a high score may mean chemotherapy is preferred.

faqs.q: Can PCI improve with chemotherapy?
faqs.a: Yes. In some patients, chemotherapy can shrink deposits and lower the PCI, which may make surgery possible later.

faqs.q: Why is small bowel involvement important?
faqs.a: Extensive small bowel involvement can make complete removal unsafe or impossible, even with a moderate PCI score.

faqs.q: Who calculates the PCI score?
faqs.a: It is calculated by the surgical oncologist, based on imaging, laparoscopy or findings during surgery.

title: Pseudomyxoma Peritonei: Symptoms and Treatment
seoTitle: Pseudomyxoma Peritonei | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Pseudomyxoma peritonei is a rare condition where jelly-like mucus fills the abdomen, often from an appendix tumour. Learn the symptoms, diagnosis.
imageAlt: Woman listening to a surgeon explain pseudomyxoma peritonei treatment
quickAnswer: Common symptoms are gradual abdominal swelling, bloating, increasing waist size, discomfort, hernias and sometimes appendicitis-like pain. CT scans and tumour markers help diagnosis. CRS removes all visible mucus and tumour, and HIPEC treats remaining cells. Outcomes are often good in experienced centres.

body.text: Pseudomyxoma peritonei (PMP) is a rare condition in which tumour cells produce large amounts of jelly-like mucus that collects in the abdomen. It most often starts from a tumour of the appendix. Although it spreads slowly, untreated mucus can build up and press on organs. The standard treatment for suitable patients is cytoreductive surgery (CRS) with HIPEC, which can offer long-term control and even cure.
What Causes PMP?

items: Most often a mucinous tumour of the appendix
Less commonly from ovarian, colon or other mucinous tumours

body.text: When the tumour ruptures or spreads, cells and mucus spread across the abdominal lining.
Common Symptoms

items: Slowly increasing abdominal size
Bloating or a feeling of fullness
Abdominal discomfort or pain
New hernia, especially near the navel or groin
Change in bowel habits
Weight gain around the abdomen despite weight loss elsewhere
Sometimes found during surgery for suspected appendicitis or an ovarian mass

body.text: How Is It Diagnosed?

items: CT scan: shows typical mucus patterns in the abdomen
MRI: may add detail
Tumour markers: CEA, CA 19-9 and CA-125 may be raised
Biopsy or surgical findings: confirm the diagnosis and grade

body.text: Grades of PMP

items: Low-grade: slow-growing, better outlook
High-grade: more aggressive behaviour

body.text: The grade influences prognosis and treatment planning.
How Is It Treated?
Cytoreductive surgery (CRS)
Removes all visible tumour and mucus, along with affected organs or peritoneal surfaces. This can be lengthy surgery.
HIPEC
Heated chemotherapy circulated in the abdomen after CRS to target remaining tumour cells.
Follow-up
Regular scans and tumour markers to detect recurrence early.
Other treatments
Systemic chemotherapy may be used for high-grade or non-resectable disease. Debulking surgery may relieve symptoms when complete removal is not possible.
Why Is Specialist Care Important?
PMP is rare and complex. Treatment in a centre experienced in peritoneal surface oncology improves the chance of complete removal and good recovery.
Key Takeaways

items: PMP is a rare mucus-producing condition.
It usually starts from the appendix.
Increasing abdominal size is a common sign.
CRS and HIPEC are the main treatment.
Experienced centres achieve better results.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Pseudomyxoma peritonei is rare, but effective treatment exists. Early referral to a specialist team can make a meaningful difference. For PMP evaluation and CRS-HIPEC care, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Is pseudomyxoma peritonei cancer?
faqs.a: It is a form of cancer, usually arising from a mucinous tumour of the appendix. Low-grade PMP grows slowly but still needs treatment.

faqs.q: Can pseudomyxoma peritonei be cured?
faqs.a: Many patients, especially with low-grade disease and complete removal, achieve long-term survival after CRS and HIPEC. Some may be considered cured.

faqs.q: Why does my abdomen keep getting bigger?
faqs.a: In PMP, mucus builds up gradually in the abdomen, causing increasing size. This needs evaluation with imaging to find the cause.

faqs.q: Can PMP come back after surgery?
faqs.a: Yes, recurrence is possible. Regular follow-up with scans and tumour markers helps detect it early, and repeat surgery may be possible.

faqs.q: How long is surgery for PMP?
faqs.a: CRS for PMP can take many hours because all visible disease must be removed. Your surgical team will explain what to expect.

faqs.q: Is chemotherapy alone effective for PMP?
faqs.a: Systemic chemotherapy has limited effect on low-grade PMP. Surgery with HIPEC is the main treatment. Chemotherapy may be used for high-grade disease.

title: Recovery After CRS and HIPEC: What to Expect
seoTitle: Recovery After HIPEC | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Recovery after CRS and HIPEC takes time. Learn what to expect in the ICU, on the ward and at home, common side effects and practical tips to regain strength.
imageAlt: Patient walking in a hospital corridor with a nurse and IV stand
quickAnswer: After CRS and HIPEC, expect ICU monitoring for a day or more, gradual return to eating, pain management, drains and tubes, and early mobilisation. Fatigue, reduced appetite and bowel changes are common for weeks. Most people return to light activities within six to eight weeks and closer to normal life by three months, depending on surgery extent.

body.text: Cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC is one of the most extensive operations in cancer care, so recovery takes time and patience. Most patients spend a short time in the ICU, followed by about one to three weeks in hospital. Full recovery at home can take two to three months. Early walking, good nutrition and close follow-up help recovery go smoothly.
In the ICU

items: Close monitoring of breathing, heart, kidneys and fluids
Pain control, often with an epidural or pain pump
Drains and a urinary catheter
Sometimes a nasogastric tube to rest the bowel

body.text: On the Ward

items: Gradual removal of tubes and drains
Slow return from fluids to soft foods
Feeding support through a vein or tube if needed
Breathing exercises and walking several times a day
Blood tests to monitor recovery and chemotherapy effects

body.text: Common Side Effects

items: Tiredness and weakness
Reduced appetite or early fullness
Nausea
Changes in bowel habits
Temporary drop in blood counts from HIPEC
Wound discomfort

body.text: Possible Complications

items: Infection
Leak from a bowel join
Bleeding
Blood clots
Fluid around the lungs
Bowel slowdown (ileus)

body.text: Your team monitors closely to catch and treat these early.
Recovery at Home
Activity
Walk daily, increasing distance gradually. Avoid heavy lifting for about six to eight weeks.
Nutrition
Eat small, frequent, protein-rich meals. Supplements may be advised.
Wound care
Keep wounds clean and dry, and watch for redness or discharge.
Emotional health
Low mood or anxiety is common after major surgery. Talk to family and your care team.
Follow-up
Regular visits, blood tests and scans. Some patients receive further chemotherapy.
When to Call Your Doctor

items: Fever or chills
Increasing abdominal pain or swelling
Persistent vomiting
Redness or discharge from the wound
Breathlessness or chest pain
Leg swelling or pain

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Recovery after CRS and HIPEC takes time.
ICU care is usually followed by one to three weeks in hospital.
Fatigue and appetite changes are common.
Walking and nutrition support recovery.
Full recovery often takes two to three months.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Recovering from CRS and HIPEC is a marathon, not a sprint. With patience, support and good follow-up, many patients return to meaningful daily lives. For CRS and HIPEC care, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: How long will I be in hospital after HIPEC?
faqs.a: Most patients stay about one to three weeks, depending on surgery extent and recovery speed. Your team will discharge you when you can eat, walk and manage pain.

faqs.q: When can I eat after CRS and HIPEC?
faqs.a: Eating usually starts gradually after the bowel begins working, often within days. Nutrition support may be given until you can eat enough.

faqs.q: Is fatigue normal after HIPEC?
faqs.a: Yes. Fatigue is very common and may last several weeks to months. Gentle activity, good nutrition and rest help energy return.

faqs.q: Will I need more chemotherapy after HIPEC?
faqs.a: Some patients do, depending on cancer type and pathology. Your oncologist will discuss whether further systemic chemotherapy is recommended.

faqs.q: When can I return to work?
faqs.a: Many people return to light work after about two to three months. It depends on the extent of surgery and the type of work.

faqs.q: What are signs of a complication at home?
faqs.a: Fever, increasing abdominal pain, vomiting, wound redness or discharge, breathlessness and leg swelling should be reported to your doctor promptly.

title: Laparoscopic vs Open Cancer Surgery: Key Differences
seoTitle: Laparoscopic vs Open Surgery | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Laparoscopic cancer surgery uses small cuts and a camera, while open surgery uses one larger incision. Learn the benefits, limits and how surgeons choose the.
imageAlt: Surgical team performing laparoscopic surgery guided by a monitor
quickAnswer: Laparoscopic surgery often means less pain, shorter hospital stay, quicker return to activity and fewer wound problems. Open surgery may be preferred for very large or complex tumours, extensive spread, multiple previous surgeries or certain cancers where evidence favours it. Cancer control remains the priority in choosing the approach.

body.text: Laparoscopic (keyhole) cancer surgery uses several small incisions, a camera and fine instruments, while open surgery uses a single larger incision. For many cancers, laparoscopic surgery offers similar cancer outcomes with less pain, smaller scars and faster recovery. However, it is not suitable for every patient or tumour, and the safest choice depends on the cancer and the surgical team's expertise.
How Does Laparoscopic Surgery Work?

items: Several small cuts, usually 0.5 to 1.5 cm
A camera shows a magnified view on a screen
Carbon dioxide gas gently inflates the abdomen for working space
The tumour is removed through a small extraction incision

body.text: How Does Open Surgery Work?

items: One larger incision gives direct access
The surgeon can see and feel tissues directly
Useful for complex or extensive procedures

body.text: Benefits of Laparoscopic Surgery

items: Less post-operative pain
Smaller scars
Shorter hospital stay
Faster return to eating and activity
Lower risk of wound infection and hernia
Less blood loss in many cases

body.text: When Open Surgery May Be Better

items: Very large tumours
Tumours involving major blood vessels or multiple organs
Extensive adhesions from previous surgery
Certain cancers where studies show better results with open surgery
Emergency situations

body.text: Is Cancer Control the Same?

For many cancers, including colorectal, stomach, kidney and endometrial cancers, studies show laparoscopic surgery achieves similar cancer outcomes when done by experienced surgeons. For some cancers, such as early cervical cancer, evidence has favoured open surgery.
Conversion to Open Surgery
Sometimes a laparoscopic operation is converted to open surgery during the procedure for safety. This is a responsible decision, not a failure.
How Is the Approach Chosen?

items: Cancer type and stage
Tumour size and location
Previous surgeries
Patient health and body type
Surgeon experience and available technology

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Laparoscopic surgery uses small incisions and a camera.
It often offers faster, less painful recovery.
Cancer outcomes are similar for many cancers.
Open surgery suits some complex cases.
Safety and cancer control guide the choice.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Both laparoscopic and open surgery have important roles in cancer care. The best approach is the one that removes the cancer safely and completely for your situation. For minimally invasive oncology assessment, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Is laparoscopic cancer surgery as effective as open surgery?
faqs.a: For many cancers, yes, when performed by experienced surgeons. Outcomes like complete removal and survival are similar. The decision depends on cancer type and stage.

faqs.q: Why might my surgeon recommend open surgery?
faqs.a: Open surgery may be safer for large, complex tumours, extensive disease, many previous operations or cancers where evidence supports it.

faqs.q: Is recovery faster after laparoscopic surgery?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Most patients have less pain, shorter hospital stays and return to normal activities sooner than after open surgery.

faqs.q: What does conversion to open surgery mean?
faqs.a: It means the surgeon switches from keyhole to open surgery during the operation to ensure safety or complete tumour removal.

faqs.q: Are there risks specific to laparoscopic surgery?
faqs.a: Rare risks include injury from instrument entry and effects of carbon dioxide gas. Overall complication rates are similar or lower than open surgery.

faqs.q: Will I have a scar after laparoscopic surgery?
faqs.a: You will have several small scars and one slightly larger cut for removing the specimen. These usually heal well and fade over time.

title: Robotic Cancer Surgery: Benefits and Limits
seoTitle: Robotic Cancer Surgery | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Robotic surgery gives surgeons 3D vision and precise instruments for complex cancer operations. Learn how it works, where it helps most, its limits.
imageAlt: Surgeon operating a robotic surgery console in an operating theatre
quickAnswer: Robotic surgery may offer greater precision, better visualisation and easier work in narrow areas, which can benefit cancers of the rectum, prostate, uterus, kidney and some head and neck sites. Recovery benefits are often similar to laparoscopic surgery. Limits include higher cost, longer setup time and availability. Cancer outcomes depend mostly on surgeon expertise and correct patient selection.

body.text: Robotic cancer surgery is a form of minimally invasive surgery where the surgeon controls robotic arms from a console. The system provides a magnified 3D view and instruments that bend and rotate more than the human wrist. The robot does not operate on its own. It helps the surgeon perform precise movements, especially in tight spaces like the pelvis.
How Does Robotic Surgery Work?

items: Small incisions are made, similar to laparoscopy
Robotic arms hold the camera and instruments
The surgeon sits at a console and controls movements
3D high-definition view with magnification
Filters hand tremor for steady movements

body.text: Where Can It Help?

items: Rectal cancer surgery in a narrow pelvis
Prostate cancer
Gynecological cancers such as endometrial cancer
Kidney cancer, especially partial kidney removal
Some stomach, esophageal and head and neck cancers

body.text: Potential Benefits

items: Precise dissection near nerves and vessels
Better ergonomics for the surgeon
Less blood loss in some procedures
Smaller incisions and less pain than open surgery
Shorter hospital stay than open surgery
Possibly better preservation of nerve function in pelvic surgery

body.text: Limitations

items: Higher cost than laparoscopic or open surgery
Not available in all hospitals
Longer setup and operating time in some cases
No sense of touch for the surgeon
Not suitable for every tumour or patient
Benefit over laparoscopy is not clear for every cancer

body.text: Is Robotic Surgery Better Than Laparoscopic Surgery?
For many cancers, outcomes are similar. Robotic surgery may have advantages in specific operations, especially deep in the pelvis. Surgeon skill and experience are more important than the platform.
Questions to Ask Your Surgeon

items: Is robotic surgery suitable for my cancer?
What are the benefits compared with laparoscopy or open surgery?
How many robotic procedures of this type have you done?
What is the cost difference?
What happens if conversion is needed?

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: The surgeon controls the robot at all times.
It provides 3D vision and precise instruments.
It may help most in narrow spaces like the pelvis.
Costs are higher than other approaches.
Surgeon expertise matters more than technology.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Robotic surgery is a valuable tool in modern cancer care, but it is one option among several. The right choice balances benefit, safety and cost for your case. For minimally invasive cancer surgery assessment, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Does the robot perform the surgery?
faqs.a: No. The surgeon controls every movement from a console. The robot translates the surgeon's hand movements into precise instrument actions.

faqs.q: Is robotic surgery safer than open surgery?
faqs.a: Robotic surgery often has smaller incisions and faster recovery. Safety depends on the operation, patient factors and surgeon experience.

faqs.q: Is robotic surgery more expensive?
faqs.a: Yes, usually. The equipment and instruments add cost. Ask your hospital for an estimate and check insurance coverage.

faqs.q: Which cancers benefit most from robotic surgery?
faqs.a: Rectal, prostate, gynecological and kidney cancers are common examples, especially where precise work in tight spaces is needed.

faqs.q: Is recovery faster after robotic surgery?
faqs.a: Recovery is often faster than after open surgery and similar to laparoscopic surgery. Individual recovery depends on the procedure and health.

faqs.q: Can every patient have robotic surgery?
faqs.a: No. Some tumours, previous surgeries or health conditions may make another approach safer. Your surgeon will advise.

title: Is Laparoscopic Surgery Safe for Cancer?
seoTitle: Is Laparoscopic Surgery Safe for Cancer | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Laparoscopic surgery is safe and effective for many cancers when done by trained surgeons. Learn what research shows, common concerns like tumour spread.
primaryKeyword: is laparoscopic surgery safe for cancer
imageAlt: Surgeon answering patient questions beside a laparoscopic instrument model
quickAnswer: Large studies have shown that laparoscopic surgery for colorectal, stomach, kidney and endometrial cancers can match open surgery for complete tumour removal, lymph node yield and survival. Benefits include less pain and faster recovery. Concerns such as tumour spread at port sites are rare with proper technique. For certain cancers, like early cervical cancer, open surgery may be preferred.

body.text: Yes, for many cancers, laparoscopic surgery is safe and offers cancer outcomes similar to open surgery when performed by trained and experienced surgeons. It follows the same cancer principles, including removing the tumour with clear margins and appropriate lymph nodes. However, it is not suitable for every cancer or patient, so careful selection is essential.
What Does Research Show?

items: Colorectal cancer: similar survival and recurrence with laparoscopy in experienced hands
Stomach cancer: good outcomes for early and many locally advanced cancers in expert centres
Kidney cancer: laparoscopic and robotic surgery widely used
Endometrial cancer: minimally invasive surgery is commonly preferred
Cervical cancer: studies have shown better outcomes with open radical hysterectomy for many cases

body.text: Common Concerns
Can laparoscopy spread cancer?
With proper oncological technique, such as using protective bags for tumour removal, the risk of port-site spread is very low.
Will the surgeon remove enough tissue?
Laparoscopic cancer surgery follows the same principles of margins and lymph node removal as open surgery.
What if something goes wrong?
Surgeons can convert to open surgery at any time if needed for safety.
When May It Not Be Suitable?

items: Very large or invasive tumours
Extensive spread within the abdomen
Severe adhesions from earlier surgeries
Some heart or lung conditions that make gas inflation risky
Cancers where evidence favours open surgery

body.text: What Makes It Safe?

items: Experienced surgeon and team
Correct patient selection
Proper equipment and technique
Willingness to convert when needed
Good post-operative care

body.text: Benefits Beyond Cancer Control

items: Less pain
Shorter hospital stay
Faster return to eating and walking
Earlier start of chemotherapy if needed
Smaller scars

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Laparoscopic surgery is safe for many cancers.
Cancer outcomes are similar to open surgery in experienced hands.
Port-site spread is rare with good technique.
Some cancers are better treated with open surgery.
Surgeon expertise is key.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Laparoscopic cancer surgery is well established and offers real recovery benefits for suitable patients. Asking questions about the approach helps you feel confident in your plan. For minimally invasive cancer surgery, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Does laparoscopic surgery increase cancer recurrence?
faqs.a: For many cancers, studies show no increase in recurrence compared with open surgery when done by experienced surgeons using proper technique.

faqs.q: Can cancer spread through the small incisions?
faqs.a: This is very rare with modern techniques, such as removing tumours in protective bags and careful handling of tissue.

faqs.q: Is laparoscopic surgery suitable for advanced cancer?
faqs.a: It depends. Some locally advanced cancers can be treated laparoscopically in expert centres. Very extensive disease may need open surgery.

faqs.q: Why is open surgery preferred for cervical cancer?
faqs.a: Research comparing approaches found better outcomes with open radical hysterectomy for many patients with early cervical cancer. Guidelines reflect this.

faqs.q: How do I know if my surgeon is experienced?
faqs.a: Ask how many similar laparoscopic cancer operations they perform and their outcomes. Experienced surgeons are open about this.

faqs.q: Does laparoscopic surgery allow faster chemotherapy?
faqs.a: Often yes. Faster recovery may allow chemotherapy to start sooner, which can be helpful in some cancers.

title: Staging Laparoscopy: Why It Is Done in Cancer Care
seoTitle: Staging Laparoscopy | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Staging laparoscopy uses a small camera to look inside the abdomen for hidden cancer spread that scans may miss. Learn why it is done, how it works.
imageAlt: Laparoscopic camera tower and monitor in an operating theatre
quickAnswer: CT, MRI and PET scans can miss small deposits on the abdominal lining or liver surface. Staging laparoscopy allows direct viewing, biopsies and fluid sampling. If hidden spread is found, the team may recommend chemotherapy first or a different plan instead of major surgery. It is usually done under general anaesthesia, often as a day-care or overnight procedure.

body.text: Staging laparoscopy is a short keyhole procedure where a surgeon inserts a camera into the abdomen to look for cancer spread that scans may not detect. It is often done before major surgery for stomach, pancreatic, esophageal, ovarian and peritoneal cancers. It helps avoid unnecessary large operations and ensures patients get the right treatment from the start.
Why Is It Needed?

items: Scans can miss deposits smaller than a few millimetres
Peritoneal spread is often hard to see on imaging
It prevents patients from undergoing major surgery that would not help
It allows accurate staging and treatment planning

body.text: Which Cancers Commonly Use It?

items: Stomach cancer
Pancreatic cancer
Esophageal and junction cancers
Ovarian cancer
Peritoneal surface malignancies before CRS and HIPEC
Some liver and bile duct cancers

body.text: How Is It Done?

items: General anaesthesia
One to three small incisions
Gas inflates the abdomen for viewing
Camera inspects the peritoneum, liver, bowel and other organs
Biopsies of suspicious areas
Peritoneal washings to check for free cancer cells

body.text: It usually takes under an hour.
What Can It Show?

items: Peritoneal deposits
Small liver surface tumours
Tumour invasion into nearby structures
Free cancer cells in fluid
Peritoneal Cancer Index for HIPEC planning

body.text: Recovery

items: Often discharged the same day or the next day
Mild pain at incision sites
Shoulder tip pain from gas, which settles quickly
Return to normal activities within a few days

body.text: How Does It Change Treatment?

items: No spread found: proceed with planned surgery
Limited spread: may consider chemotherapy then reassess, or CRS-HIPEC in suitable cases
Extensive spread: systemic treatment instead of major surgery

body.text: Risks
Staging laparoscopy is generally safe. Rare risks include bleeding, infection or injury to organs.
Key Takeaways

items: Staging laparoscopy finds spread scans can miss.
It prevents unnecessary major surgery.
It is quick with fast recovery.
Biopsies and washings guide treatment.
It is common before stomach, pancreatic and peritoneal surgery.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Staging laparoscopy is a small step that can make a big difference to the right treatment plan. It ensures each patient's path is based on accurate information. For cancer staging and surgical planning, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Why do I need a laparoscopy if I already had a scan?
faqs.a: Scans can miss very small deposits on the abdominal lining. Laparoscopy allows direct viewing and biopsy, giving more accurate staging.

faqs.q: Is staging laparoscopy a major operation?
faqs.a: No. It is a short keyhole procedure, usually under an hour, with quick recovery. Many patients go home the same or next day.

faqs.q: What happens if cancer spread is found?
faqs.a: Your team may recommend chemotherapy first, a different surgery or other treatment. It helps avoid a major operation that may not benefit you.

faqs.q: Can staging laparoscopy and major surgery be done together?
faqs.a: Sometimes. If no spread is found, the surgeon may proceed with the main operation in the same sitting, depending on the plan.

faqs.q: What are peritoneal washings?
faqs.a: Saline is washed into the abdomen and collected to check for free cancer cells. A positive result affects staging and treatment decisions.

faqs.q: Is staging laparoscopy painful?
faqs.a: Pain is usually mild and managed with simple painkillers. Shoulder tip pain from the gas is common for a day or two.

title: Recovery After Laparoscopic Cancer Surgery
seoTitle: Recovery After Laparoscopic Surgery | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Recovery after laparoscopic cancer surgery is often faster than open surgery. Learn what to expect in hospital and at home, how to manage pain.
imageAlt: Woman walking in a sunny garden a week after laparoscopic surgery
quickAnswer: Expect mild pain at incision sites, shoulder tip pain from gas, tiredness and some bloating. Most people leave hospital within two to five days after major laparoscopic cancer surgery. Light activities resume within one to two weeks, and heavier work or exercise after four to six weeks, as advised by your surgeon.

body.text: Recovery after laparoscopic (keyhole) cancer surgery is usually quicker and less painful than after open surgery. Many patients walk the same or next day, start eating within a day or two and go home within a few days, depending on the operation. Full internal healing still takes several weeks, so gradual return to activity is important.
In Hospital

items: Early walking, often within hours or by the next day
Gradual start of fluids and soft foods
Pain control with tablets
Removal of drains or catheter if used
Breathing exercises

body.text: Common Symptoms

items: Pain at small incision sites
Shoulder tip pain from carbon dioxide gas
Bloating and gas
Tiredness
Mild nausea
Changes in bowel habits

body.text: Most settle within days to weeks.
Recovery at Home
Week 1

items: Walk short distances several times a day
Eat small, balanced meals
Keep wounds clean and dry
Rest when tired

body.text: Weeks 2 to 3

items: Increase activity gradually
Return to light office work for many people
Avoid lifting heavy objects

body.text: Weeks 4 to 6

items: Return to most normal activities
Resume exercise gradually if your surgeon agrees
Attend follow-up and discuss pathology results

body.text: Wound Care

items: Keep dressings clean
Shower as advised, pat wounds dry
Watch for redness, swelling or discharge
Avoid tight clothing over wounds

body.text: Driving
Most people can drive when they can brake suddenly without pain and are off strong painkillers, often after one to two weeks. Check with your surgeon.
Nutrition

items: Protein-rich foods support healing
Stay hydrated
Include fibre gradually to prevent constipation

body.text: When to Call Your Doctor

items: Fever above 38 degrees Celsius
Increasing abdominal pain or swelling
Vomiting or inability to eat
Redness, pus or bleeding from wounds
Leg pain or swelling
Breathlessness or chest pain

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Laparoscopic surgery often means faster recovery.
Shoulder tip pain from gas is common and temporary.
Early walking and good nutrition help healing.
Avoid heavy lifting for several weeks.
Report warning signs promptly.

body.text: Final Thoughts

A smoother recovery is one of the main benefits of laparoscopic cancer surgery, but internal healing still needs time. Following your team's advice helps you get back to life safely. For minimally invasive cancer surgery care, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: How soon can I go home after laparoscopic cancer surgery?
faqs.a: It depends on the operation. Many patients go home within two to five days. Smaller procedures may allow same-day or next-day discharge.

faqs.q: Why does my shoulder hurt after laparoscopic surgery?
faqs.a: Gas used during surgery can irritate the diaphragm, causing referred pain in the shoulder. It usually settles within a few days.

faqs.q: When can I return to work?
faqs.a: Many people return to desk work within two to three weeks. Physical jobs may need four to six weeks or longer. Ask your surgeon.

faqs.q: When can I lift heavy objects?
faqs.a: Avoid heavy lifting for about four to six weeks to allow internal healing and reduce hernia risk. Your surgeon will guide you.

faqs.q: Is constipation normal after surgery?
faqs.a: Yes, due to painkillers and reduced activity. Drink fluids, walk and add fibre gradually. A mild laxative may be advised.

faqs.q: When will I know my final cancer results?
faqs.a: Pathology results usually take one to two weeks. Your surgeon will discuss them at follow-up and plan any further treatment.
