title: Blood in Stool: Piles or Colorectal Cancer?
seoTitle: Blood in Stool Piles or Cancer | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Blood in stool is often due to piles, but it can also be a sign of colorectal cancer. Learn the differences, red flag symptoms and when a colonoscopy is needed.
primaryKeyword: blood in stool piles or cancer
imageAlt: Man speaking privately with a doctor about rectal bleeding
quickAnswer: Piles usually cause bright red blood on toilet paper or dripping after stools, often with itching or a lump. Colorectal cancer may cause dark or mixed blood, change in bowel habits, weight loss, tiredness from anaemia and abdominal pain. Anyone with rectal bleeding should be examined. A colonoscopy is often advised to rule out cancer.

body.text: Blood in stool is commonly caused by piles (haemorrhoids) or anal fissures, but it can also be a warning sign of colorectal cancer. The two can look similar, so it is not safe to assume bleeding is due to piles without a proper examination, especially if you are over 40, have other symptoms or have a family history of bowel cancer.
Common Causes of Blood in Stool

items: Piles (haemorrhoids)
Anal fissure
Colorectal polyps
Colorectal cancer
Inflammatory bowel disease
Infections
Diverticular disease

body.text: Bleeding From Piles

items: Bright red blood
Blood on toilet paper or dripping into the pan
Often painless
May have itching or a lump near the anus
Often related to constipation or straining

body.text: Bleeding From Colorectal Cancer

items: Dark red or maroon blood, or blood mixed with stool
Black, tarry stools in some cases
May be hidden and only found on tests

body.text: Red Flag Symptoms
See a doctor promptly if bleeding comes with:

items: Change in bowel habits lasting more than a few weeks
Feeling of incomplete emptying
Unexplained weight loss
Tiredness or breathlessness from anaemia
Abdominal pain or a lump
Narrow, pencil-like stools
Age over 40 to 45
Family history of colorectal cancer or polyps

body.text: How Is It Evaluated?

items: Digital rectal examination
Proctoscopy: to see piles or fissures
Colonoscopy: examines the full colon and allows biopsy or polyp removal
Blood tests: to check for anaemia
Stool tests: for hidden blood in some cases

body.text: Why Not Assume It Is Piles?

Piles are common, and people often delay seeing a doctor. But piles and colorectal cancer can occur together. Missing cancer can delay treatment. A simple examination and, when needed, colonoscopy give peace of mind.
Key Takeaways

items: Blood in stool is often from piles, but not always.
Dark or mixed blood may suggest a deeper cause.
Bowel habit change and weight loss are red flags.
Colonoscopy helps rule out cancer.
Never assume bleeding is only piles without a check.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Rectal bleeding is a symptom that deserves attention, not embarrassment. Early evaluation often brings reassurance, and if cancer is found, early treatment works best. For colorectal assessment, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: How can I tell if bleeding is from piles or cancer?
faqs.a: You cannot reliably tell at home. Piles usually cause bright red blood on paper, while cancer may cause darker or mixed blood with other symptoms. A doctor's examination is needed.

faqs.q: Should young people worry about blood in stool?
faqs.a: Piles and fissures are common causes in younger people, but colorectal cancer is increasing in young adults. Persistent bleeding or other symptoms should be checked at any age.

faqs.q: Do I need a colonoscopy for rectal bleeding?
faqs.a: Many people do, especially if over 40, with red flag symptoms or a family history. Your doctor will decide after examination.

faqs.q: Can piles turn into cancer?
faqs.a: No. Piles do not turn into cancer. However, both conditions can exist together, so bleeding should not be blamed on piles without proper evaluation.

faqs.q: What does black stool mean?
faqs.a: Black, tarry stool may indicate bleeding higher in the digestive tract, such as the stomach. It needs urgent medical evaluation.

faqs.q: Can colon polyps cause bleeding?
faqs.a: Yes. Some polyps bleed. Removing polyps during colonoscopy can prevent them from developing into cancer.

title: Colonoscopy: Preparation and What to Expect
seoTitle: Colonoscopy Preparation | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Colonoscopy examines the whole colon and can find and remove polyps. Learn how to prepare, what happens during the test, sedation, recovery.
imageAlt: Nurse explaining colonoscopy preparation to a patient in an endoscopy suite
quickAnswer: Before colonoscopy, you follow a low-residue diet and drink a bowel preparation solution to empty the colon. The procedure usually takes 20 to 45 minutes, often under sedation. Polyps can be removed and biopsies taken during the test. Most people go home the same day and return to normal activities the next day.

body.text: A colonoscopy is a test that uses a thin, flexible tube with a camera to examine the inside of the large bowel (colon and rectum). It is used to find the cause of symptoms like bleeding, to screen for colorectal cancer and to remove polyps before they turn into cancer. Good bowel preparation is the key to an accurate test.
Why Is Colonoscopy Done?

items: Rectal bleeding or blood in stool
Change in bowel habits
Unexplained anaemia
Abdominal pain or weight loss
Colorectal cancer screening
Follow-up after polyp removal or cancer surgery
Family history of colorectal cancer

body.text: How to Prepare
A few days before

items: Tell your doctor about all medicines, especially blood thinners, diabetes medicines and iron tablets
Stop iron tablets if advised
Avoid seeds, nuts and high-fibre foods

body.text: The day before

items: Follow a clear or low-residue diet as advised
Drink the bowel preparation solution exactly as instructed
Expect frequent loose stools
Stay near a toilet and drink plenty of clear fluids

body.text: On the day

items: Do not eat
Follow instructions on when to stop drinking
Arrange for someone to accompany you home if sedation is used

body.text: What Happens During the Test?

items: You lie on your side
Sedation is given if planned
The scope is gently inserted through the anus
Air or carbon dioxide inflates the colon for a clear view
The doctor examines the lining
Polyps may be removed and biopsies taken

body.text: After the Test

items: Rest until sedation wears off
Mild bloating or cramping from air is common
Slight bleeding may occur if polyps were removed
Resume normal diet unless told otherwise
Avoid driving for the rest of the day if sedated

body.text: Possible Risks
Colonoscopy is generally safe. Rare risks include bleeding, perforation (a tear in the bowel) and reactions to sedation.
Results

items: Normal: no further tests may be needed for some years
Polyps: removed and sent for analysis, with follow-up based on results
Cancer or suspicious areas: biopsy results guide next steps

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Colonoscopy examines the whole large bowel.
Good bowel preparation is essential.
Polyps can be removed during the test.
Sedation makes it comfortable for most.
It is key for detecting and preventing colorectal cancer.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Colonoscopy may seem daunting, but it is one of the most powerful tools for preventing and detecting colorectal cancer. Good preparation makes it quick and effective. For colorectal evaluation, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Is colonoscopy painful?
faqs.a: Most people feel little discomfort, especially with sedation. Some cramping or bloating may occur during or after the test.

faqs.q: Why is bowel preparation so important?
faqs.a: A clean colon allows the doctor to see the lining clearly. Poor preparation can hide polyps or cancer and may mean repeating the test.

faqs.q: Can I take my regular medicines before colonoscopy?
faqs.a: Most medicines can be continued, but blood thinners, diabetes medicines and iron may need adjustment. Always check with your doctor beforehand.

faqs.q: How long does colonoscopy take?
faqs.a: The procedure usually takes 20 to 45 minutes. Including preparation and recovery, plan for a few hours at the hospital.

faqs.q: What happens if a polyp is found?
faqs.a: It is usually removed during the same procedure and sent for testing. Results guide how often you need repeat colonoscopy.

faqs.q: At what age should I have a screening colonoscopy?
faqs.a: Guidelines often recommend starting colorectal cancer screening around 45 to 50 for average-risk adults. People with family history or symptoms may need it earlier.

title: Living With a Colostomy or Ileostomy
seoTitle: Living With Colostomy | Dr Varadharajan V
description: A stoma can feel overwhelming at first, but most people adapt well. Learn the difference between colostomy and ileostomy, daily care, diet tips.
imageAlt: Man with a stoma chatting confidently with friends at a cafe
quickAnswer: A colostomy usually produces thicker stool and is often on the left side. An ileostomy produces looser output and is usually on the right side. Daily care involves emptying and changing the pouch, protecting the skin and staying hydrated. A stoma nurse teaches care skills. Many temporary stomas can be reversed after a few months.

body.text: A stoma is an opening on the abdomen created during bowel surgery so that stool can leave the body into a pouch. A colostomy is made from the large bowel, and an ileostomy from the small bowel. Stomas can be temporary, to protect a healing bowel join, or permanent. With good guidance, most people return to work, travel, exercise and social life.
Colostomy vs Ileostomy
Colostomy

items: Made from the colon
Output is usually semi-formed to formed
Often on the left side of the abdomen

body.text: Ileostomy

items: Made from the small intestine (ileum)
Output is more liquid
Usually on the right side
Higher risk of dehydration

body.text: Why Is a Stoma Needed?

items: To protect a new bowel join after rectal cancer surgery
When the rectum and anus are removed
In emergencies such as bowel blockage or perforation
After some complex cancer surgeries

body.text: Daily Stoma Care

items: Empty the pouch when it is one-third to half full
Change the pouch or base plate as advised
Clean the skin gently with water and dry well
Measure the stoma regularly in the early weeks, as it shrinks
Check skin for redness or irritation

body.text: Diet Tips
Early weeks

items: Eat small, regular meals
Chew well
Introduce high-fibre foods slowly

body.text: Ongoing

items: Drink plenty of fluids, especially with an ileostomy
Add salty foods or oral rehydration if advised
Be careful with foods that may block the stoma, like popcorn, nuts or fibrous vegetables, if chewed poorly
Note foods that cause gas or odour

body.text: Living a Normal Life

items: Work: most people return to work
Clothing: pouches are discreet under normal clothes
Exercise: walking, yoga and swimming are possible; avoid heavy lifting early on
Travel: carry extra supplies
Intimacy: possible with communication and support

body.text: When Is Reversal Possible?
Temporary stomas are often reversed after healing, usually several weeks to months after surgery or after chemotherapy. Tests check that the join has healed before reversal.
When to Seek Help

items: No output for many hours with pain or vomiting
Very high output with signs of dehydration
Stoma turning dark or black
Bleeding that does not stop
Severe skin irritation
Bulging around the stoma (parastomal hernia)

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: A stoma diverts stool into a pouch.
Colostomy output is thicker; ileostomy is looser.
Stoma nurses teach essential care skills.
Hydration is especially important with ileostomy.
Many stomas can be reversed.

body.text: Final Thoughts

A stoma is a change, not the end of a full life. With knowledge, practice and support, most people regain confidence quickly. For colorectal cancer surgery and stoma planning, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Is a stoma permanent?
faqs.a: Not always. Many stomas are temporary and reversed after healing. Permanent stomas are needed when the rectum and anus are removed.

faqs.q: Will people notice my stoma pouch?
faqs.a: Modern pouches are slim and discreet. Most people will not notice under normal clothing. Odour-proof pouches help with confidence.

faqs.q: Can I eat normally with a stoma?
faqs.a: Most people return to a varied diet. Some foods may cause gas or blockage, so introduce them gradually and chew well.

faqs.q: How often should I change the pouch?
faqs.a: It depends on the system. Some pouches are changed daily, others every few days. Your stoma nurse will advise.

faqs.q: Why is hydration important with an ileostomy?
faqs.a: Ileostomy output contains more water and salt, which increases the risk of dehydration. Drink plenty of fluids and use rehydration solutions if advised.

faqs.q: When can a temporary stoma be reversed?
faqs.a: Usually after several weeks to months, once the bowel join has healed and any chemotherapy is complete. Tests confirm readiness.

title: Rectal Cancer: Sphincter-Saving Surgery Explained
seoTitle: Sphincter Saving Surgery | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Sphincter-saving surgery removes rectal cancer while keeping the anal muscles, avoiding a permanent stoma for many patients. Learn who qualifies and what to.
imageAlt: Oncologist explaining a pelvic anatomy model to a patient
quickAnswer: Sphincter-saving surgery, such as low anterior resection or intersphincteric resection, may be possible when the tumour is far enough from the anal muscles to achieve clear margins and the sphincter function is good. Treatment before surgery may shrink the tumour. A temporary stoma is often created to protect the join. Bowel habits may change afterward but often improve over months.

body.text: Sphincter-saving surgery removes rectal cancer while preserving the anal sphincter muscles that control bowel movements. This allows many patients to avoid a permanent colostomy. Advances in surgical techniques, along with chemotherapy and radiation before surgery, have made sphincter preservation possible even for many low rectal tumours.
Types of Sphincter-Saving Surgery
Low anterior resection (LAR)
Removes the affected part of the rectum and joins the colon to the remaining rectum or anal canal.
Ultra-low anterior resection
For tumours very low in the rectum, joining the colon close to the anus.
Intersphincteric resection
Removes part of the inner sphincter muscle for very low tumours while preserving the outer muscle.
Total mesorectal excision (TME)
A key technique that removes the rectum along with its surrounding fatty tissue and lymph nodes, lowering recurrence risk.
Who May Be Suitable?

items: Tumour not involving the anal sphincter muscles
Ability to achieve clear surgical margins
Good pre-surgery bowel control
Favourable response to chemoradiation, if given

body.text: When Is a Permanent Stoma Needed?

items: Tumour invading the sphincter muscles
Very poor sphincter function before surgery
Clear margins cannot be achieved otherwise

body.text: In such cases, abdominoperineal resection with a permanent colostomy may be recommended.
Role of Treatment Before Surgery

Chemoradiation or chemotherapy before surgery can shrink tumours, improving the chance of sphincter preservation and lowering recurrence. In some patients with complete response, a watch-and-wait approach may be discussed in expert centres.
Temporary Stoma
A temporary ileostomy is often created to protect the new join while it heals. It is usually reversed after several weeks to months.
Life After Surgery
Low anterior resection syndrome (LARS) is common and may include:

items: Frequent or urgent bowel movements
Clustering of stools
Incontinence episodes

body.text: These often improve over months with diet changes, medicines and pelvic floor exercises.
Key Takeaways

items: Sphincter-saving surgery avoids a permanent stoma for many.
TME is the key technique for rectal cancer.
Pre-surgery treatment can improve preservation chances.
A temporary stoma often protects the join.
Bowel changes usually improve with time.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Many people with rectal cancer can keep normal bowel function with modern surgery. A careful plan balances cancer control with quality of life. For rectal cancer surgery evaluation, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Can I avoid a permanent stoma with rectal cancer?
faqs.a: Many patients can, especially if the tumour does not involve the anal muscles. Your surgeon will assess tumour location and response to treatment.

faqs.q: What is total mesorectal excision?
faqs.a: It is a surgical technique that removes the rectum along with its surrounding fat and lymph nodes in one intact package, reducing the risk of cancer returning.

faqs.q: Why is a temporary stoma needed?
faqs.a: It diverts stool away from the new join while it heals, lowering the risk of serious leak complications. It is usually reversed later.

faqs.q: What is low anterior resection syndrome?
faqs.a: It refers to bowel changes after rectal surgery, like frequency, urgency or clustering. It often improves over months with management.

faqs.q: Can chemotherapy and radiation help save the sphincter?
faqs.a: Yes. Treatment before surgery can shrink the tumour, increasing the chance of sphincter preservation and improving cancer control.

faqs.q: What is watch and wait for rectal cancer?
faqs.a: In some patients with complete response to chemoradiation, close monitoring without immediate surgery may be considered in expert centres.

title: Colorectal Cancer in Young Adults: Signs Not to Ignore
seoTitle: Colon Cancer in Young Adults | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Colorectal cancer is rising in people under 50. Learn the warning signs young adults often dismiss, possible risk factors and why persistent symptoms need.
imageAlt: Young office worker pausing at his desk with abdominal discomfort
quickAnswer: Warning signs include rectal bleeding, change in bowel habits, abdominal pain, unexplained weight loss, tiredness from anaemia and a feeling of incomplete emptying. Young adults with these symptoms, especially if they persist for more than a few weeks, should see a doctor. A colonoscopy may be advised to find the cause.

body.text: Colorectal cancer is often thought of as a disease of older adults, but cases in people under 50 have been increasing in many countries. Young adults are more likely to dismiss symptoms as piles, stress or stomach upset, which can delay diagnosis. Recognising warning signs and getting checked early can make a big difference.
Why Is It Increasing in Young People?
The exact reasons are not fully known. Possible contributors include:

items: Diets high in processed and red meat
Low fibre intake
Obesity
Physical inactivity
Sugary drinks
Changes in gut bacteria
Smoking and alcohol

body.text: Genetics also play a role in some cases.
Warning Signs

items: Blood in stool or rectal bleeding
Change in bowel habits, such as diarrhoea, constipation or narrower stools
Abdominal pain or cramping
Feeling that the bowel does not empty fully
Unexplained weight loss
Fatigue or breathlessness from anaemia
Iron deficiency without clear cause

body.text: Who Is at Higher Risk?

items: Family history of colorectal cancer or polyps
Inherited conditions like Lynch syndrome or familial adenomatous polyposis
Inflammatory bowel disease such as ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease
Obesity and sedentary lifestyle

body.text: Why Is Diagnosis Delayed?

items: Symptoms are blamed on piles or diet
Young people may avoid doctors
Doctors may not suspect cancer in younger patients
Embarrassment about bowel symptoms

body.text: How Is It Diagnosed?

items: Physical examination including rectal exam
Blood tests for anaemia
Colonoscopy with biopsy
CT scan to check spread if cancer is found

body.text: Is Treatment Different?
Treatment is based on stage, similar to older patients. It may include surgery, chemotherapy and radiation. Young patients may also need genetic testing and fertility counselling before treatment.
How to Lower Risk

items: Eat more fibre, vegetables, fruits and whole grains
Limit processed and red meat
Maintain a healthy weight
Stay active
Avoid smoking and limit alcohol
Know your family history

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Colorectal cancer is rising in under-50s.
Rectal bleeding and bowel changes need attention.
Symptoms are often wrongly blamed on piles.
Family history increases risk.
Early evaluation leads to better outcomes.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Being young does not rule out colorectal cancer. Listening to your body and seeking help early is the best protection. For colorectal assessment, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Can people in their 20s and 30s get colorectal cancer?
faqs.a: Yes. While less common, colorectal cancer can occur in young adults. Persistent bowel symptoms should be checked regardless of age.

faqs.q: Why is colorectal cancer increasing in young adults?
faqs.a: The exact cause is unclear. Diet, obesity, inactivity, gut bacteria changes and other lifestyle factors are being studied as possible contributors.

faqs.q: Should young adults get screening?
faqs.a: Routine screening usually starts around 45 to 50 for average risk. Those with family history or genetic conditions may need earlier screening.

faqs.q: Is rectal bleeding in young people always piles?
faqs.a: No. Piles are common, but bleeding can also be caused by polyps or cancer. Persistent bleeding should be evaluated.

faqs.q: Does family history matter?
faqs.a: Yes. Having a close relative with colorectal cancer, especially at a young age, increases risk. Share this with your doctor.

faqs.q: Will treatment affect fertility?
faqs.a: Some treatments, like pelvic radiation and certain chemotherapy, can affect fertility. Young patients should discuss fertility preservation before treatment.

title: Can Stage 4 Cancer Be Operated On?
seoTitle: Stage 4 Cancer Surgery | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Surgery is sometimes possible in stage 4 cancer, especially with limited spread. Learn when it may help, what oligometastatic disease means.
imageAlt: Surgical and medical oncologists reviewing PET-CT scans together
quickAnswer: Surgery may be considered in stage 4 cancer when spread is limited to a few sites (oligometastatic disease), the cancer responds well to chemotherapy, all disease can be removed safely, and the patient is fit for surgery. Examples include colorectal cancer with liver or lung spread and selected peritoneal cancers treated with CRS and HIPEC. Decisions are made by a multidisciplinary tumour board.

body.text: Yes, in some cases. Stage 4 cancer means the cancer has spread beyond its original site to distant organs. Traditionally, surgery was rarely offered at this stage, but for selected patients with limited spread, removing both the primary tumour and the metastases can offer long-term control and, in some cancers, even cure. Surgery may also be used to relieve symptoms.
What Is Oligometastatic Disease?
It means cancer has spread to only a few locations, usually one to five sites. In some cancers, treating these limited sites with surgery or other local treatments may improve outcomes.
Where Surgery May Help in Stage 4

items: Colorectal cancer: removal of liver or lung metastases
Peritoneal spread: CRS and HIPEC for selected cancers
Neuroendocrine tumours: removal of liver metastases
Kidney cancer: removal of the kidney and limited metastases in some cases
Ovarian cancer: cytoreductive surgery for advanced disease
Sarcomas: lung metastases in selected patients

body.text: When Is Surgery Considered?

items: Limited and removable metastases
Good response to chemotherapy or other treatment
Stable disease over time
Good overall health
Agreement of the tumour board

body.text: When Is Surgery Not Helpful?

items: Widespread metastases
Rapidly progressing disease
Poor general health
When surgery would not improve survival or quality of life

body.text: Palliative Surgery
Even when cure is not possible, surgery may help relieve:

items: Bowel blockage
Bleeding
Severe pain
Fluid build-up

body.text: Combined Treatment
Stage 4 treatment often combines:

items: Systemic therapy (chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy)
Surgery
Radiation or ablation
Supportive and palliative care

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Stage 4 does not always rule out surgery.
Limited spread may be treatable surgically.
Colorectal liver metastases are a common example.
Response to chemotherapy guides decisions.
Tumour boards decide the best approach.

body.text: Final Thoughts

A stage 4 diagnosis is serious, but options may exist beyond chemotherapy alone. A specialist review can clarify whether surgery could play a role. For advanced cancer surgery evaluation, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Is stage 4 cancer always incurable?
faqs.a: Not always. Some stage 4 cancers with limited spread, such as colorectal cancer with liver metastases, can be cured with combined treatment including surgery.

faqs.q: What does oligometastatic mean?
faqs.a: It means cancer has spread to only a few sites. Treating these sites with surgery or other local treatments may improve outcomes in some cancers.

faqs.q: Why is chemotherapy given before surgery in stage 4 cancer?
faqs.a: It helps shrink tumours, tests how the cancer responds and may make surgery possible or more effective.

faqs.q: Can surgery improve quality of life in stage 4 cancer?
faqs.a: Yes. Palliative surgery can relieve symptoms like blockage, bleeding or pain, even when cure is not the goal.

faqs.q: Who decides if surgery is possible?
faqs.a: A multidisciplinary tumour board, including surgeons, oncologists and radiologists, reviews your case and recommends the best plan.

faqs.q: Should I get a second opinion for stage 4 cancer?
faqs.a: It can be helpful, especially when considering complex surgery. A specialist centre may offer additional options.

title: Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy: Why Treatment Comes Before Surgery
seoTitle: Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is given before surgery to shrink tumours and treat hidden spread. Learn why it is used, which cancers benefit and how it affects.
imageAlt: Woman receiving chemotherapy through an IV line in a day-care unit
quickAnswer: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy may allow smaller or less extensive surgery, improve the chance of complete tumour removal, treat microscopic spread early and provide information about tumour response. Surgery is usually planned a few weeks after the last cycle, once the body recovers. Some patients also receive radiation before surgery.

body.text: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is chemotherapy given before surgery. Its aims are to shrink the tumour, make surgery easier or more effective, treat cancer cells that may have spread unseen and show how well the cancer responds to treatment. It is commonly used in breast, stomach, esophageal, rectal, ovarian, pancreatic and some other cancers.
Why Give Chemotherapy First?
Shrink the tumour
Smaller tumours may be easier and safer to remove.
Allow organ-preserving surgery
For example, breast-conserving surgery instead of mastectomy, or sphincter-saving surgery in rectal cancer.
Treat hidden spread
Early treatment may target microscopic cancer cells elsewhere in the body.
Test response
How the tumour responds helps guide further treatment and predict outcomes.
Select patients for surgery
In aggressive cancers, it helps identify those who will benefit from surgery.
Cancers Where It Is Commonly Used

items: Breast cancer
Stomach and esophageal cancer
Rectal cancer, often with radiation
Ovarian cancer
Pancreatic cancer in selected cases
Bladder cancer
Some sarcomas and head and neck cancers

body.text: What Happens During Treatment?

items: Chemotherapy is given in cycles over weeks to months
Regular blood tests and scans check response
Side effects are monitored and managed
The surgical team stays involved in planning

body.text: Timing of Surgery
Surgery is usually scheduled a few weeks after chemotherapy ends to allow recovery of blood counts and general health.
Common Side Effects

items: Tiredness
Nausea
Hair loss with some drugs
Low blood counts and infection risk
Mouth sores
Numbness in hands and feet with certain drugs

body.text: What If the Tumour Does Not Shrink?
Your team may change the treatment plan, proceed with surgery earlier or consider other options. Not responding does not always mean surgery is impossible.
Key Takeaways

items: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is given before surgery.
It can shrink tumours and treat hidden spread.
It may allow less extensive surgery.
Response helps guide future treatment.
Surgery follows after a recovery period.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Starting with chemotherapy can feel like delaying surgery, but it is often a carefully planned step that improves outcomes. Your team will explain why it suits your case. For multidisciplinary surgical planning, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Does chemotherapy before surgery delay treatment?
faqs.a: No. Chemotherapy is treatment in itself. It starts attacking the cancer immediately, and surgery follows as part of the planned sequence.

faqs.q: What is the difference between neoadjuvant and adjuvant chemotherapy?
faqs.a: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is given before surgery. Adjuvant chemotherapy is given after surgery to reduce the risk of recurrence.

faqs.q: Can neoadjuvant chemotherapy make the tumour disappear?
faqs.a: In some patients, the tumour shrinks so much that no cancer is found at surgery. This is called a complete response and is often a good sign.

faqs.q: How long after chemotherapy is surgery done?
faqs.a: Usually a few weeks after the last cycle, to allow the body to recover. Your team will schedule based on blood counts and health.

faqs.q: Will I still need chemotherapy after surgery?
faqs.a: It depends on the cancer type and how it responded. Some patients need further treatment after surgery.

faqs.q: Does neoadjuvant chemotherapy make surgery riskier?
faqs.a: Generally no, when timing is planned well. Surgery is scheduled after recovery to reduce complications.

title: What Is a Tumour Board and How Does It Help You?
seoTitle: What Is a Tumour Board | Dr Varadharajan V
description: A tumour board is a meeting where cancer specialists review your case together to plan the best treatment. Learn who attends, what they discuss.
imageAlt: Multidisciplinary tumour board reviewing scans around a conference table
quickAnswer: A tumour board typically includes surgical oncologists, medical oncologists, radiation oncologists, radiologists, pathologists and other specialists as needed. They review your diagnosis and stage, then recommend whether surgery, chemotherapy, radiation or a combination should come first. Your doctor then discusses the recommendation with you.

body.text: A tumour board, also called a multidisciplinary team meeting, is a regular meeting where specialists from different areas of cancer care review individual patient cases together. They discuss scans, pathology and medical history to agree on the best treatment plan. This team approach helps ensure that every option is considered and that care is well coordinated.
Who Attends a Tumour Board?

items: Surgical oncologist: assesses whether surgery is possible and appropriate
Medical oncologist: advises on chemotherapy, targeted therapy or immunotherapy
Radiation oncologist: advises on radiation therapy
Radiologist: reviews scans and imaging
Pathologist: explains biopsy and tissue findings
Others as needed: gastroenterologists, gynecologists, nurses, dietitians, palliative care and genetic counsellors

body.text: What Is Discussed?

items: Type and stage of cancer
Imaging and biopsy results
Overall health and other conditions
Treatment options and sequence
Clinical trial possibilities
Patient preferences shared by the treating doctor

body.text: Why Does It Matter?

items: Combines expertise from many specialists
Reduces the chance of missing treatment options
Helps plan the correct order of treatments
Improves coordination between departments
Supports evidence-based decisions
Studies suggest multidisciplinary care can improve outcomes in many cancers

body.text: When Are Cases Discussed?

items: At diagnosis, before starting treatment
After major test results or surgery
When cancer recurs or does not respond
When considering complex surgery such as CRS and HIPEC

body.text: Do Patients Attend?
Usually not. The treating doctor presents your case and later explains the recommendations to you. You remain part of the decision and can ask questions.
How Can You Prepare?

items: Share all previous reports and scans
Tell your doctor about your priorities and concerns
Ask whether your case has been discussed at a tumour board
Request a clear explanation of the recommendations

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: A tumour board brings cancer specialists together.
It reviews scans, pathology and health details.
It recommends the best treatment sequence.
Multidisciplinary care can improve outcomes.
You remain involved in final decisions.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Knowing your case has been reviewed by a team of specialists can bring confidence and peace of mind. It ensures your treatment plan is thoughtful and complete. For multidisciplinary cancer surgical care, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Why is my case being discussed at a tumour board?
faqs.a: Tumour boards help ensure the best treatment plan by combining input from different cancer specialists. It is a standard part of good cancer care.

faqs.q: Can I attend the tumour board meeting?
faqs.a: Patients usually do not attend. Your doctor presents your case and then discusses the recommendations with you in detail.

faqs.q: Does a tumour board make the final decision?
faqs.a: It makes a recommendation. The final decision is made by you and your doctor together, considering your preferences.

faqs.q: How long does a tumour board review take?
faqs.a: Cases are usually reviewed at scheduled meetings, often weekly. Your doctor will update you soon after the discussion.

faqs.q: Can a tumour board suggest a clinical trial?
faqs.a: Yes. If a suitable clinical trial is available, the board may recommend it as an option to discuss with you.

faqs.q: Is a tumour board the same as a second opinion?
faqs.a: Not exactly. It is a team review within a hospital. You can still seek an external second opinion if you wish.

title: Palliative Surgery: Goals and Expectations
seoTitle: Palliative Surgery | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Palliative surgery aims to relieve symptoms and improve quality of life in advanced cancer, not to cure it. Learn when it is used, common procedures.
imageAlt: Senior man resting peacefully in a garden with his grandchild
quickAnswer: Palliative surgery may be considered for bowel obstruction, bleeding, perforation, blocked bile ducts, difficulty swallowing, painful tumours or fluid build-up. It aims to restore comfort and function. Not every patient will benefit, so careful discussion about goals, recovery and alternatives such as stents or medicines is essential.

body.text: Palliative surgery is surgery performed to relieve symptoms, prevent complications and improve quality of life in people with advanced cancer, rather than to cure the disease. It can help with problems such as bowel blockage, bleeding, pain or difficulty eating. The decision to proceed is based on balancing expected benefits with risks and the patient's goals.
Goals of Palliative Surgery

items: Relieve pain or pressure
Restore eating or bowel function
Control bleeding
Prevent emergencies
Improve independence and comfort
Allow continuation of other treatments

body.text: Common Palliative Procedures
Bowel obstruction
Bypass surgery or a stoma to relieve blockage.
Bleeding tumours
Removal of the bleeding part or procedures to control it.
Swallowing difficulty
Feeding tubes or bypass procedures for blocked food pipe or stomach.
Blocked bile duct
Surgical bypass if stents are not suitable.
Fluid build-up
Drainage procedures or catheters for recurrent ascites or pleural fluid.
Tumour causing pain or wounds
Removal to relieve symptoms.
Alternatives to Surgery

items: Endoscopic stents
Radiation for bleeding or pain
Medicines to control symptoms
Drainage procedures by interventional radiology
Palliative care support

body.text: These may be less invasive and more suitable for some patients.
How Are Decisions Made?

items: Patient goals and preferences
Expected benefit and duration of relief
Overall health and fitness
Risks and recovery time
Life expectancy
Availability of less invasive options

body.text: Open conversations with your surgeon, oncologist and palliative care team help guide the choice.
What to Expect
Recovery depends on the procedure and your health. Some procedures offer quick relief, while others need longer recovery. Your team will explain realistic expectations.
Key Takeaways

items: Palliative surgery relieves symptoms, not cure.
It can help with blockage, bleeding and pain.
Less invasive alternatives may be available.
Decisions focus on quality of life.
Patient goals guide every choice.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Palliative surgery is about comfort, dignity and quality of life. When chosen thoughtfully, it can make a real difference in daily living. For advanced cancer surgical care, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: What is the difference between curative and palliative surgery?
faqs.a: Curative surgery aims to remove all cancer. Palliative surgery aims to relieve symptoms and improve quality of life when cure is not possible.

faqs.q: Is palliative surgery worth the risk?
faqs.a: It depends on your symptoms, overall health and goals. Your team will discuss expected benefits and risks so you can make an informed decision.

faqs.q: Can palliative surgery extend life?
faqs.a: In some cases, relieving complications like bowel blockage may extend life and allow further treatment. The main aim is comfort and function.

faqs.q: Are there non-surgical options for symptom relief?
faqs.a: Yes. Stents, radiation, medicines and drainage procedures may relieve symptoms with less recovery time. Your team will consider these first when suitable.

faqs.q: Will I need to stay in hospital long?
faqs.a: It depends on the procedure. Some patients go home in a few days, while larger operations need longer stays.

faqs.q: Who should be involved in the decision?
faqs.a: You, your family, your surgeon, oncologist and palliative care team. Sharing your goals and concerns helps make the best choice.

title: Recurrent Cancer: Is Surgery an Option?
seoTitle: Recurrent Cancer Surgery | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Surgery may still be possible when cancer comes back, especially if the recurrence is limited. Learn when repeat surgery helps, what tests are needed.
imageAlt: Woman discussing recurrent cancer surgery options with her oncologist
quickAnswer: Surgery for recurrent cancer may be considered when the recurrence is localised, there is no widespread spread, complete removal is possible, enough time has passed since previous treatment and the patient is fit. Imaging, biopsy and tumour board review help decide. Other options include chemotherapy, radiation, targeted therapy or clinical trials.

body.text: When cancer returns after treatment, it is called recurrence. Surgery may still be an option, especially when the recurrence is limited to one area and can be completely removed. For some cancers, such as colorectal, ovarian, peritoneal, sarcoma and some head and neck cancers, repeat surgery can offer long-term control. Each case needs careful assessment.
Types of Recurrence

items: Local recurrence: cancer returns at the original site
Regional recurrence: cancer returns in nearby lymph nodes
Distant recurrence: cancer appears in other organs

body.text: Local and limited regional recurrences are more likely to be treated with surgery.
Cancers Where Surgery May Help

items: Colorectal cancer, including liver and lung recurrences
Ovarian cancer with a longer gap since last treatment
Peritoneal recurrences in selected patients, sometimes with CRS and HIPEC
Head and neck cancers with local recurrence
Soft tissue sarcomas
Some breast cancer recurrences in the chest wall or breast

body.text: Factors That Guide Decisions

items: Location and extent of recurrence
Time since initial treatment
Previous surgery and radiation
Tumour biology and response to earlier treatment
Patient fitness and preferences

body.text: How Is Recurrence Evaluated?

items: CT, MRI or PET-CT scans
Tumour markers
Biopsy to confirm recurrence
Tumour board discussion

body.text: Challenges of Repeat Surgery

items: Scar tissue from previous surgery
Changes from earlier radiation
Need for more complex reconstruction
Possibly longer recovery

body.text: Experienced surgical teams are better able to manage these challenges.
Other Treatment Options

items: Chemotherapy, targeted therapy or immunotherapy
Radiation or re-irradiation in selected cases
Local ablation for small liver or lung lesions
Clinical trials
Palliative and supportive care

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Recurrent cancer may still be treatable with surgery.
Limited, localised recurrences are best suited.
A longer gap since treatment improves outcomes.
Repeat surgery can be more complex.
Tumour boards help choose the best approach.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Cancer coming back is difficult news, but it does not always mean the end of curative options. A thorough review can uncover treatment paths worth exploring. For recurrent cancer surgical evaluation, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Can recurrent cancer be cured?
faqs.a: Sometimes. For limited recurrences that can be fully removed, surgery may offer long-term control or cure, depending on cancer type and biology.

faqs.q: Is repeat surgery riskier?
faqs.a: It can be more complex because of scar tissue and previous radiation. Experienced teams carefully plan to reduce risks.

faqs.q: Why does the time since first treatment matter?
faqs.a: A longer gap often suggests slower-growing cancer, which may respond better to surgery and other treatments.

faqs.q: What tests are needed for recurrent cancer?
faqs.a: Scans such as CT, MRI or PET-CT, tumour markers and often a biopsy to confirm recurrence and check spread.

faqs.q: Will I need chemotherapy as well?
faqs.a: Often yes. Chemotherapy or other systemic treatment may be given before or after surgery to improve control.

faqs.q: Should I get a second opinion?
faqs.a: A second opinion from a specialist centre can be helpful, especially when considering complex repeat surgery.

title: Breast Cancer Screening: Self-Exam and Mammogram
seoTitle: Breast Cancer Screening | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Breast cancer screening helps detect cancer early when treatment works best. Learn about breast self-awareness, clinical exams, mammograms, when to start.
imageAlt: Woman beside a radiographer at a mammography machine in a diagnostic centre
quickAnswer: Women should know how their breasts normally look and feel and report changes promptly. Clinical breast examination is useful during regular check-ups. Mammograms are generally recommended for women from around 40 to 50, depending on the guideline and personal risk, every one to two years. Women with a strong family history or BRCA mutations may need earlier and more frequent screening, sometimes with MRI.

body.text: Breast cancer screening aims to find cancer early, often before symptoms appear, when treatment is simpler and more effective. Screening includes breast self-awareness, clinical breast examination by a doctor and mammography. The right schedule depends on age, family history and personal risk factors.
Breast Self-Awareness
Rather than strict monthly routines, experts encourage knowing what is normal for you.
How to check

items: Look in a mirror for changes in shape, size or skin
Raise your arms and check for dimpling or puckering
Feel each breast and armpit with flat fingers in circles
Check while lying down and standing
Look for nipple changes or discharge

body.text: Changes to report

items: New lump or thickening
Skin dimpling or redness
Nipple turning inward
Bloody discharge
Swelling or lump in the armpit
Persistent pain in one area

body.text: Clinical Breast Examination
A doctor or trained health worker examines the breasts and armpits. This can be part of routine health check-ups.
Mammogram
A low-dose X-ray of the breasts that can detect tumours too small to feel.
When to start
Many guidelines suggest starting between 40 and 50 for average-risk women, with intervals of one to two years. Your doctor can help you decide based on your risk.
What to expect

items: Each breast is gently compressed for a few seconds
It may feel uncomfortable but is brief
Avoid deodorant or powder on the day

body.text: Ultrasound and MRI

items: Ultrasound: often used for younger women, dense breasts or to evaluate a lump
MRI: used for high-risk women along with mammograms

body.text: Who Needs Earlier Screening?

items: Close relatives with breast or ovarian cancer
Known BRCA1, BRCA2 or other gene mutations
Previous chest radiation at a young age
Personal history of breast cancer or certain benign conditions

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Screening finds cancer early.
Know your normal and report changes.
Mammograms are key from around 40 to 50.
High-risk women may need earlier screening.
Ultrasound and MRI support screening in some cases.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Screening is one of the most powerful ways to protect your health. Talk to your doctor about the schedule that fits your risk. For breast cancer evaluation, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: At what age should I start mammograms?
faqs.a: Many guidelines recommend starting between 40 and 50 for average-risk women. Women with higher risk may start earlier. Discuss timing with your doctor.

faqs.q: Is a breast self-exam enough?
faqs.a: Self-awareness helps you notice changes, but it does not replace clinical exams and mammograms, which can find cancers too small to feel.

faqs.q: Are mammograms safe?
faqs.a: Yes. Mammograms use a low dose of radiation. The benefit of early detection outweighs the very small risk for most women.

faqs.q: Do mammograms hurt?
faqs.a: They can be uncomfortable for a few seconds because of compression. Scheduling after your period may reduce tenderness.

faqs.q: What if I have dense breasts?
faqs.a: Dense breasts can make mammograms harder to read. Your doctor may suggest additional ultrasound or MRI.

faqs.q: Do men need breast screening?
faqs.a: Routine screening is not recommended for men, but any breast lump in a man should be checked by a doctor.

title: Pap Smear and HPV Test: Cervical Cancer Screening
seoTitle: Pap Smear and HPV Test | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Pap smears and HPV tests can find cervical changes before they become cancer. Learn how they work, when to start, how often to test and what abnormal results.
imageAlt: Gynecologist talking with a woman before a cervical screening check-up
quickAnswer: Cervical screening is usually recommended from around age 21 to 25, depending on guidelines. Pap smears may be done every three years, while HPV testing, alone or combined with a Pap smear, may be done every five years from about age 30. Abnormal results do not mean cancer but need follow-up, often with colposcopy.

body.text: A Pap smear checks cells from the cervix for abnormal changes, while an HPV test looks for high-risk types of human papillomavirus, the main cause of cervical cancer. Both tests can detect problems early, often years before cancer develops. Regular screening is one of the most effective ways to prevent cervical cancer.
What Is a Pap Smear?
A doctor gently collects cells from the cervix using a small brush or spatula. The cells are examined under a microscope for abnormal changes.
What Is an HPV Test?
It checks the same or a similar sample for high-risk HPV types linked to cervical cancer. HPV infection is common and often clears on its own, but persistent infection can cause cell changes.
When Should Screening Start?
Guidelines differ, but common recommendations include:

items: Starting between 21 and 25 years
Pap smear every three years in younger women
HPV testing every five years from around 30
Continuing until about 65 if previous results are normal

body.text: India's national programmes may also use visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) in some settings.
How to Prepare

items: Schedule when you are not on your period
Avoid intercourse, douching or vaginal medicines for 48 hours before
Wear comfortable clothing

body.text: What Happens During the Test?

items: You lie on an examination table
A speculum is gently inserted
Cells are collected from the cervix
It takes a few minutes and may cause mild discomfort

body.text: Understanding Results

items: Normal: routine screening continues
HPV positive with normal cells: repeat testing or further evaluation
Abnormal cells: colposcopy to look closely at the cervix and take biopsies if needed

body.text: Most abnormal results are due to minor changes that can be monitored or treated simply.
Treatment of Pre-Cancerous Changes

items: Monitoring if changes are mild
Removal of abnormal tissue with procedures like LEEP or cryotherapy

body.text: Prevention

items: HPV vaccination, ideally before sexual activity begins
Regular screening even after vaccination
Avoid smoking

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Pap and HPV tests prevent cervical cancer.
Screening usually starts in the early twenties.
HPV testing is often every five years after 30.
Abnormal results need follow-up, not panic.
HPV vaccination adds strong protection.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Cervical cancer is largely preventable with regular screening and vaccination. A few minutes every few years can protect your health. For gynecological cancer evaluation, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Is a Pap smear painful?
faqs.a: It may cause mild discomfort or pressure but is usually not painful. The test takes only a few minutes.

faqs.q: How often should I have a Pap smear?
faqs.a: Often every three years for younger women, or HPV testing every five years from around 30. Your doctor will advise based on your history.

faqs.q: Does a positive HPV test mean I have cancer?
faqs.a: No. HPV is common and often clears on its own. A positive result means closer monitoring or further tests to check for cell changes.

faqs.q: Do I need screening if I had the HPV vaccine?
faqs.a: Yes. The vaccine does not protect against all HPV types, so regular screening is still important.

faqs.q: What is colposcopy?
faqs.a: It is a procedure where the doctor uses a magnifying device to look closely at the cervix and take biopsies of abnormal areas.

faqs.q: When can I stop cervical screening?
faqs.a: Many guidelines suggest stopping around 65 if previous results have been normal. Your doctor will guide you.

title: Oral Cancer Screening: Who Needs It and How It Works
seoTitle: Oral Cancer Screening | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Oral cancer screening is a quick mouth examination that can find early cancer and pre-cancerous patches. Learn who should be screened, how it is done.
imageAlt: Dentist examining a patient mouth with a light and mirror
quickAnswer: Oral cancer screening takes a few minutes. A doctor or dentist checks for white or red patches, ulcers, lumps and areas of thickening, and feels the neck for enlarged lymph nodes. People who use tobacco, gutka, areca nut or alcohol should be screened regularly. Any suspicious area may need a biopsy.

body.text: Oral cancer screening is a simple visual and physical examination of the mouth, lips, tongue, gums and throat to look for signs of cancer or pre-cancerous changes. In India, where mouth cancer is common due to tobacco and areca nut use, regular screening can help find problems early, when treatment is most successful.
Who Should Be Screened?

items: Tobacco smokers or chewers
Users of gutka, paan, khaini or areca nut
Regular alcohol users
People over 30 with risk habits
Those with a history of pre-cancerous lesions
People with reduced mouth opening
Anyone with a non-healing mouth sore

body.text: India's national programmes recommend oral screening for adults, especially those with risk factors.
What Happens During Screening?

items: The doctor looks inside your mouth with a light
Checks the lips, gums, cheeks, tongue, floor of mouth and palate
Feels for lumps in the mouth and neck
Asks about habits and symptoms

body.text: It is painless and quick.
What Are Doctors Looking For?

items: White patches (leukoplakia)
Red patches (erythroplakia)
Non-healing ulcers
Lumps or thickened areas
Reduced mouth opening (oral submucous fibrosis)
Enlarged neck lymph nodes

body.text: What If Something Is Found?

items: A biopsy may be taken
Some pre-cancerous lesions are monitored closely
Others may be removed
If cancer is diagnosed, staging tests and treatment planning follow

body.text: How to Self-Check at Home

items: Use a mirror and good light
Check lips, gums, cheeks and tongue, including underneath
Look at the roof and floor of your mouth
Feel for lumps in the mouth and neck
Do this once a month

body.text: Report any change lasting more than two weeks.
How Can You Lower Your Risk?

items: Quit tobacco and areca nut in all forms
Limit alcohol
Maintain oral hygiene
Visit a dentist regularly
Eat fruits and vegetables

body.text: Key Takeaways

items: Oral cancer screening is quick and painless.
Tobacco and areca nut users need regular checks.
White and red patches can be pre-cancerous.
Biopsy confirms suspicious findings.
Monthly self-checks help early detection.

body.text: Final Thoughts

A few minutes of screening can save lives, especially for those with risk habits. Early detection makes treatment simpler and more successful. For oral cancer assessment, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: How often should I get oral cancer screening?
faqs.a: If you use tobacco or areca nut, regular screening at least once a year is advisable. Your doctor may suggest more frequent checks if you have pre-cancerous lesions.

faqs.q: Can a dentist do oral cancer screening?
faqs.a: Yes. Dentists often check for signs of oral cancer during routine visits. Suspicious findings are referred for biopsy and specialist review.

faqs.q: Is oral cancer screening painful?
faqs.a: No. It is a simple visual and touch examination that takes a few minutes.

faqs.q: What is leukoplakia?
faqs.a: It is a white patch in the mouth that cannot be wiped off. Some leukoplakias can become cancerous, so they need monitoring or treatment.

faqs.q: Should non-smokers get screened?
faqs.a: People without risk factors may not need frequent screening but should report any persistent mouth changes. Regular dental visits help.

faqs.q: What happens if a biopsy shows pre-cancer?
faqs.a: Treatment may include stopping tobacco, close monitoring or removing the lesion. Early treatment can prevent progression to cancer.

title: Colorectal Cancer Screening Options Explained
seoTitle: Colorectal Cancer Screening | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Colorectal cancer screening can find polyps before they turn into cancer. Learn about stool tests, colonoscopy and CT colonography, when to start.
imageAlt: Couple reading a colorectal screening leaflet in a clinic waiting area
quickAnswer: Stool tests such as FIT detect hidden blood and are done yearly. Colonoscopy examines the whole colon and allows polyp removal, usually every ten years if normal. CT colonography is a scan-based option every five years. Any positive stool test or abnormal scan needs a colonoscopy. The best test is the one you are willing to do regularly.

body.text: Colorectal cancer screening aims to find cancer early or detect polyps before they turn into cancer. Options include stool-based tests, colonoscopy and CT colonography. Many guidelines recommend average-risk adults begin screening around age 45 to 50. People with a family history or certain conditions may need earlier and more frequent screening.
Why Screen?

items: Most colorectal cancers start as polyps
Removing polyps prevents cancer
Early cancers are easier to treat
Many early cancers have no symptoms

body.text: Screening Options
Faecal immunochemical test (FIT)

items: Detects hidden blood in stool
Done at home
Usually repeated every year
A positive result needs colonoscopy

body.text: Stool DNA test

items: Detects blood and abnormal DNA
Done every one to three years where available

body.text: Colonoscopy

items: Examines the entire colon
Polyps can be removed during the test
Needs bowel preparation and often sedation
Usually every ten years if normal

body.text: CT colonography

items: Uses a CT scan to create images of the colon
Needs bowel preparation but no sedation
Usually every five years
Abnormal results need colonoscopy

body.text: Flexible sigmoidoscopy

items: Examines the lower part of the colon
Less commonly used alone

body.text: When Should Screening Start?

items: Average risk: often from 45 to 50
Family history: often earlier, such as 40 or ten years before the youngest affected relative
Genetic syndromes or inflammatory bowel disease: much earlier and more frequently

body.text: Who Is at Higher Risk?

items: Family history of colorectal cancer or polyps
Lynch syndrome or familial adenomatous polyposis
Ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease
Previous polyps or colorectal cancer

body.text: Symptoms Mean Testing, Not Screening
If you have rectal bleeding, change in bowel habits, weight loss or anaemia, you need diagnostic tests, not routine screening. See a doctor promptly.
Key Takeaways

items: Screening prevents and detects colorectal cancer early.
FIT is simple and done yearly.
Colonoscopy can remove polyps.
Screening often starts at 45 to 50.
Higher-risk people need earlier screening.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Colorectal cancer is one of the most preventable cancers through screening. Choose a test with your doctor and stay on schedule. For colorectal assessment, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Which colorectal screening test is best?
faqs.a: The best test is one you will do regularly. Colonoscopy is the most complete, while FIT is simple and done at home. Discuss options with your doctor.

faqs.q: At what age should I start screening?
faqs.a: Many guidelines suggest starting at 45 to 50 for average-risk adults. Those with family history or other risks may need to start earlier.

faqs.q: What happens if my stool test is positive?
faqs.a: A positive FIT means blood was detected. You will need a colonoscopy to find the cause, which may be polyps, piles or other conditions.

faqs.q: How often should I have a colonoscopy?
faqs.a: If normal, usually every ten years for average-risk adults. People with polyps or higher risk may need more frequent colonoscopies.

faqs.q: Can CT colonography replace colonoscopy?
faqs.a: It is an option for some people, but abnormal findings still need colonoscopy. It cannot remove polyps.

faqs.q: Should young people with symptoms wait for screening age?
faqs.a: No. Symptoms like bleeding, bowel changes or weight loss should be evaluated at any age.

title: Tumour Markers: What They Can and Cannot Tell You
seoTitle: Tumour Markers: What They Tell You | Dr Varadharajan V
description: Tumour markers like CEA, CA-125 and PSA can help monitor cancer, but they are not reliable for diagnosing it alone. Learn how they are used.
imageAlt: Doctor reviewing a blood test report showing tumour marker values
quickAnswer: Tumour markers can support diagnosis, track how well treatment works and help spot recurrence during follow-up. They cannot confirm or rule out cancer by themselves. A raised marker needs interpretation along with symptoms, scans and biopsy. Normal markers do not guarantee absence of cancer.

body.text: Tumour markers are substances in the blood or other body fluids that may be raised in some cancers. Common examples include CEA, CA-125, CA 19-9, AFP and PSA. They are useful for monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence in certain cancers, but they are not reliable for diagnosing cancer on their own because they can be raised in non-cancerous conditions and normal in some cancers.
Common Tumour Markers

items: CEA: colorectal and some other GI cancers
CA-125: ovarian cancer
CA 19-9: pancreatic and bile duct cancers
AFP: liver cancer and some testicular cancers
PSA: prostate cancer
CA 15-3: breast cancer monitoring
Beta-hCG: some testicular and gestational cancers
Thyroglobulin: thyroid cancer follow-up

body.text: What Can Tumour Markers Do?

items: Support a diagnosis when combined with other findings
Provide a baseline before treatment
Show how well treatment is working
Help detect recurrence during follow-up
Sometimes give prognostic information

body.text: What Can They Not Do?

items: Confirm cancer without imaging or biopsy
Rule out cancer when normal
Replace screening tests for most people
Always pinpoint the cancer type

body.text: Why Can Markers Be Misleading?
False positives
Markers can rise due to:

items: Infections or inflammation
Liver or kidney disease
Smoking (CEA)
Menstruation, endometriosis or fibroids (CA-125)
Bile duct blockage (CA 19-9)
Prostate enlargement or infection (PSA)

body.text: False negatives
Some cancers do not produce markers, so levels may be normal even when cancer is present.
How Are They Used in Follow-Up?
After cancer treatment, doctors may check markers at regular intervals. A steadily rising level may prompt scans to look for recurrence. Trends over time matter more than a single value.
Should Healthy People Get Tumour Marker Tests?
Generally not as a routine screening tool, except in specific situations such as PSA discussions for some men. Random testing can cause unnecessary worry and tests.
Key Takeaways

items: Tumour markers support but do not confirm diagnosis.
They are most useful for monitoring treatment.
Non-cancer conditions can raise markers.
Normal markers do not rule out cancer.
Trends matter more than single values.

body.text: Final Thoughts

Tumour markers are helpful tools when used correctly. Interpreting them with your doctor avoids unnecessary worry and supports good decisions. For cancer evaluation and follow-up, you can consult Dr. Varadharajan, a surgical oncologist in Chennai.

faqs.q: Does a high CEA mean I have cancer?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. CEA can be raised by smoking, inflammation, liver disease and other conditions. Further tests are needed to find the cause.

faqs.q: Can CA-125 diagnose ovarian cancer?
faqs.a: No. CA-125 can be raised in non-cancerous conditions and normal in some early cancers. It is used along with ultrasound and other findings.

faqs.q: Should I get tumour markers as part of a health check-up?
faqs.a: Routine tumour marker testing is not recommended for most healthy people because it can cause false alarms. Discuss screening needs with your doctor.

faqs.q: Why does my doctor check markers after surgery?
faqs.a: To track whether levels return to normal and to monitor for recurrence over time. Rising levels may prompt further tests.

faqs.q: My marker is slightly high. Should I worry?
faqs.a: A slightly raised level may be due to other conditions. Your doctor will consider symptoms, history and may repeat the test or order imaging.

faqs.q: Can tumour markers tell the stage of cancer?
faqs.a: They may give some information, but staging is mainly based on imaging, surgery and pathology results.
